chapters.title: Session 1: Where do good ideas come from?
chapters.summary: Where ideas come from, how to generate and evaluate them, and how ideas evolve through learning from failure.

pages.title: Where do good ideas come from?

blocks.text: Every great business starts with a good idea that provides the impetus for you to make your enterprise happen. The question is where do these ideas come from?

They come from thinking: from you thinking of something that other people really want or need. Perhaps the question should be more explicit: where do *good* ideas come from, how do you know they are good, and how do you know it is a good idea *for me*? It is the power of your idea that will ultimately attract interest from stakeholders, customers and end users.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

items: understand the different ways that ideas arise and how to evaluate and develop them
reflect on your own experiences and the examples and approaches provided to generate ideas
recognise that ideas evolve and can lead to more ideas about different parts of a business

blocks.text: You may well have a good idea, but does that make you an entrepreneur? The term is troublesome to define: does it describe a type of person, or a way of doing business? Is it something you are born with or something you can develop? Entrepreneurship and enterprise are closely related. These two definitions underpin the course.
Entrepreneurs are those persons (business owners) who seek to generate value, through the creation or expansion of economic activity, by identifying and exploiting new products, processes or markets.

Entrepreneurs are defined by their actions (not the size of organization they work for). They create and/or exploit change for profit, by innovating, accepting risk and moving resources to areas of higher return.

**Enterprise** is an alternative term for a business or firm, as in 'small and medium sized enterprise' (SME). It includes **social enterprises**: trading organisations that serve a primary social purpose and can take a variety of legal forms.
blocks.title: Key terms

blocks.text: An **intrapreneur** is a salaried employee in a larger company; the profits and risks of their work go to their employer.
In these definitions you will hopefully recognise yourself, or the possibility that you can become an entrepreneur if you have an idea and you know how to exploit it.

cards.back: A person who seeks to generate value by creating or expanding economic activity, identifying and exploiting new products, processes or markets.
An alternative term for a business or firm, e.g. an SME. Includes social enterprises.
A trading organisation that serves a primary social purpose.
A salaried employee in a larger company; profits and risks go to the employer.

blocks.text: Throughout the course you will learn through the experiences of real entrepreneurs who are developing and growing their own ventures. They will describe some of the key decisions they made, and why.

items: Claudio Marturano, Nubis Aviation Training
Emma Prince, Evolve Intervention
Nick Allen, Flo and Vie
Alex Bond, CEO of Fresh Check

blocks.alt: Still from the video introducing the four entrepreneurs
blocks.caption: Video 1

blocks.title: Video 1: Who are you and what is your enterprise?
blocks.note: Each of the four entrepreneurs introduces themselves. Claudio Marturano founded Nubis Aviation, a training organisation for aviation maintenance personnel, after 14 years in the industry. Emma Prince directs Evolve Intervention, an early intervention service in Essex supporting children and young people through group work, one-to-one support and work with schools and families. Nick Allen runs Flo and Vie, producing his wife's designs first on cards and now on luxury silk scarves. Alex Bond co-founded Fresh Check with colleagues from Imperial College London to help food producers test their hygiene.

blocks.text: There are many potential sources of ideas. Some fairly common examples include:

items: spotting an opportunity (e.g. a gap in the market)
experiencing a problem and looking for a solution for it (e.g. an invention)
being able to do something that others can't (e.g. using a talent)
being prepared to do something others don't want to or can't do (e.g. cleaning)
having something that others might need or want (e.g. investing in plant or machinery for hire)

blocks.text: You may have a sense of where our entrepreneurs came up with their ideas from their short biographies. Next, they confirm it in their own words.

blocks.title: Video 2: Where did the idea come from?
blocks.note: The four entrepreneurs explain where their ideas came from. Alex Bond: colleagues won an award for a business detecting fungi in potatoes, so he and fellow PhD students in chemical biology wanted to do something similar that would make a difference. Nick Allen: his interior-designer wife's designs went onto cards, were taken to markets, and a suggestion box prompted many people to say 'put them on silk scarves'. Emma Prince: years working with children in Essex schools showed many going without effective intervention because of tight budgets. Claudio Marturano: as chief engineer of an airline responsible for training 200+ maintenance staff, he could not find a training provider that met his needs.

blocks.title: Activity 1: Inspiration for a business
blocks.prompt: Watch the video on the four entrepreneurs talking about their ideas and make notes on your initial impressions of each of them. Think about how they represent their idea(s). Did they try something that worked and just run with it, or was it something they could already do? Perhaps they saw an opportunity to apply something in a new area. Or maybe they started developing knowledge and skills that they could later turn into a business.
blocks.hint: For each person, note the source: experience, skill, a frustration, feedback or an opportunity.
blocks.model: You may share experiences with the entrepreneurs: a background, talent or area of expertise applied to a problem, or involvement in a family business that revealed an opportunity. Your idea may develop an area you already work in, or apply it somewhere new. There is no one path that is sure to result in an idea or an entrepreneur.
points: Ideas often come from personal or professional experience of a problem
Existing expertise or skills can be applied to a need others have
Feedback from customers can steer an idea in a new direction
There is no single path to an idea or to becoming an entrepreneur

blocks.text: Having listened to others and taken time to reflect on your own ideas, you might have started to see patterns emerging.

items: The idea may solve a problem, perhaps one encountered in your personal or professional life.
It might be something the entrepreneurs are well placed to solve because they have the necessary expertise.
They may have fresh insight on how to improve something, or access to expertise from elsewhere.

blocks.text: Some ideas go beyond problem solving. By seeing a possibility that others do not, opportunities can come around in the most surprising ways. Your idea may arise from something you are passionate about, such as a cause, issue or interest you simply must share, or a particular capability that others seek.
Writers on enterprise tend to differentiate between innovation and enterprise. Not everyone who comes up with an innovative new idea, like an inventor, is an entrepreneur.

The entrepreneur is the person who turns an innovative idea into commercial ends or, in the case of a social entrepreneur, solves a particular social problem. Sometimes the inventor and entrepreneur are one and the same person, but not always.

James Dyson is a classic example of someone who had an idea and was also able to create it in reality. But having an idea and successfully building a product or company on the back of it does not always happen. When talking about where ideas come from, we are talking about innovation, and next you will explore the sources of innovation.

blocks.q: Which description best fits an entrepreneur rather than only an inventor?
options: Someone who comes up with a new invention
Someone who turns an innovative idea into commercial ends or solves a social problem
Someone who works for a large company
blocks.explain: The entrepreneur turns an innovative idea into commercial ends (or, for a social entrepreneur, solves a social problem). The inventor and entrepreneur may or may not be the same person.

blocks.text: Peter Drucker, a well-known management consultant, educator and writer on business and entrepreneurship, suggested that innovation may originate in three ways: **internally**, **externally**, or the **'bright idea'**.

blocks.alt: Diagram of sources of innovation: internal, external and the bright idea, each with examples
blocks.caption: Figure 1 Origins of innovation

blocks.text: Internal examples: an unexpected happening, an incongruous happening, a need for improvement in a process, changes in the industry, its structure or the market. External examples: changes in population demographics, changes in society (perception, mood or meaning), new types of knowledge.

pages.title: Finding ideas or ideas finding you

blocks.text: When looking at Drucker's sources, you might think of your idea as solving a persistent problem, or perhaps as taking a good idea from somewhere and applying it in a different context. Technology continues to present opportunities to do things differently, to do them better, or even to do things that were not possible before.

blocks.q: Drucker suggested innovation can originate internally, externally, or as a 'bright idea'.
blocks.explain: These are the three sources of innovation in Figure 1.

blocks.q: 'Changes in population demographics' is which kind of source of innovation?
blocks.explain: Demographic change is an external source; an unexpected or incongruous happening is internal.

blocks.title: Activity 2: Where are the opportunities to innovate?
blocks.prompt: Group the sources of innovation (the 21 listed, plus any of your own) in relation to whether they are internal, external or the elusive 'bright idea'. Use Drucker's Table 1: internal (an unexpected happening; an incongruous happening; a need for improvement in a process; changes in the industry, its structure or the market), external (changes in population demographics; changes in society, perception, mood or meaning; new types of knowledge) and bright idea.
blocks.model: Take internal sources and 'incongruities' as an example: they arise when you apply your experience and knowledge to things that don't feel quite right, often in a sector you know well or feel passionate about. Personal or professional life events can be important sources. Solving a persistent problem, imitating an idea from elsewhere or introducing new technology are other routes, and 'insider knowledge' lets you see possibilities others miss. The 'bright idea' and the external environment are not mutually exclusive, and several of our entrepreneurs' ideas arose from frustration that leads people to seek change.
points: Internal sources include your own work, studies, hobbies, frustrations and incongruities you notice
External sources include demographics, society's mood, regulations, technology and market change
A 'bright idea' is not mutually exclusive with the other two
Insider knowledge and spotting change quickly give an advantage

blocks.text: The aim of this course is to give you a deeper understanding of your own motivation, to zoom in on the source of your own idea. Ideas rarely emerge fully formed and are subject to almost constant refinement. Being able to spot where you can make important improvements is the key.
Sometimes you may be too close to your own ideas, and this is when looking at what others do can provide insights into your own situation.

Ideas from nowhere are exceedingly rare. Most come from experiences, positive and negative, and they may not register unless you are alert to them. The extent to which you care about them provides the impetus to act.

Thinking about the source of an idea can help assess your existing ideas or even develop new ones. Your idea may just be a starting point, and you should be alert to many more that will occur to you. New ideas will also require evaluation to select the best options for you.

cards.back: Actively noticing, watching, listening, perceiving, experiencing something.
Asking relevant questions.
The behaviour that makes you ask why, how, where and when things happen as they do.
Linking objects, people, concepts, data and ideas to see what results.
Making connections between one thing and another, e.g. possible solutions to a problem.
Developing ideas to the point where they have form.

blocks.text: Later in the course you will return to these skills in practical activities.

Is there such a thing as an 'ideas person'? This course assumes not, and nor does it assume that being enterprising is a trait you are born with. People can and do learn how to develop ideas. Those who appear good at solving problems or identifying opportunities have learned to do so.

People are exposed to different sets of opportunities. These differences create diversity in views, attitudes and approaches, which result in different ideas. Being entrepreneurial is understood as having the ability to take advantage of differences (Blundel et al., 2018).

blocks.q: This course assumes that being enterprising is a trait you are born with.
blocks.explain: The course assumes people can and do learn how to develop ideas.

blocks.alt: Black and white photograph of James Dyson from above, surrounded by tools, building something
blocks.caption: Figure 3 James Dyson

blocks.text: James Dyson was a product designer. He studied design at the Royal College of Art and, through contacts, worked for entrepreneur Jeremy Fry, who favoured a 'hands-on' approach to design and problem solving.

While renovating his house, Dyson encountered industrial extraction fans. Frustrated by the poor suction of the vacuum he used to tidy up, he wondered whether a solution from industry might work in a domestic setting. A few thousand prototypes later, a bagless domestic vacuum appeared on the market. The account ignores many technical aspects, but it demonstrates the value of learning.

blocks.title: Video 3: What makes an inventor tick?
blocks.note: James Dyson offers his views on being an inventor. There is never a 'Eureka moment': you start with an often very bad idea, build lots of prototypes and end up with something quite different that works. He likes 'wrong thinking', starting with the opposite of the correct way to do something to push thinking down a different path. Key qualities are curiosity, patience with testing, and dogged determination, like a rubber ball that bounces back. He advises building a working model, then going to a good patent agent, and criticises patent renewal fees as a tax on innovation and the shortage of UK engineers.

blocks.text: Reduce the invention to practice: build a working model to prove it works, then take it, with your drawings, to a good patent agent. Dyson's advice is to go and make it yourself rather than trying to persuade disinterested manufacturers.
blocks.title: From Dyson's video

blocks.text: Dyson's source of inspiration, or perhaps his frustration, turned into an opportunity. If others felt as he did about those poor experiences then surely there was an opportunity. New or better solutions can come from:

items: simplifying what is there
adding to what is there
emphasising different attributes
making something available in one place that otherwise customers would have to seek in many different places

blocks.text: In other words, ideas are born from context; they are not fixed.

Although you may perceive things in one way and see a new approach, this does not necessarily mean others will share your vision or view your idea as better. Changes and adaptation are likely, sometimes because your own view changes, sometimes the context, or even the way you perceive it.
Testing your ideas against others is important. The Dyson example, which took many prototypes before getting it right, illustrates this.

blocks.q: What does the Dyson prototype story mainly illustrate?
options: Good ideas arrive in a single flash
Testing and adapting an idea repeatedly is important
Prototypes are unnecessary if the idea is good
blocks.explain: It took many prototypes before getting it right: testing ideas against others is important.

pages.title: Activity 3: How ideas change over time

blocks.title: Video 4: Changing ideas
blocks.note: The entrepreneurs describe how their ideas changed. Nick Allen: they had designs people liked and just tried a market; customers' suggestions steered them to silk scarves. Claudio Marturano: the concept stayed the same but the plan changed dramatically, helped by the Open University MBA. Emma Prince: it started as mentoring and coaching and evolved as schools asked for education coaching, tuition and family work. Alex Bond: a smart food label seemed an obvious benefit, but big manufacturers found packaging too slim-margin for any label, so they developed a spray product with the same technology.

blocks.title: Activity 3: How ideas change over time
blocks.prompt: Watch Video 4. As you listen to the entrepreneurs, think about what reasons, if any, they gave for changing course.
blocks.model: Ideas can arise from many places: internally (a talent or ability), from experiences and frustrations, or from challenges you perceive as opportunities. These can all change over time. Evolution is common because when ideas meet potential customers or users, they challenge your assumptions, and feedback on likes and dislikes leads to new insights.
points: Customer feedback (e.g. suggestions to use silk scarves) led to a new product
Market demand pulled the business into new services (schools asking for more)
Cost and price realities made the original product unviable (the label was too expensive)
Core technology or concept was kept while the application changed

blocks.text: Ideas arise from internal and external sources and through different experiences. Often the simplest ideas and solutions are the best, but behind the apparent simplicity lie some very practical challenges. This section explores tools and techniques that may help.
Design thinking

'Design' has become a fashionable way to approach problem solving, and designers are seen as a great source of ideas. Dyson applied what is now called 'design thinking' before it was fashionable. Drawing on the experience of others helps you understand a challenge; it is often the mix of experience, and being able to 'see' how an idea from one area addresses an issue in another, that provides novel ways of thinking.

'Framing' is the ability to recognise the type of issue in hand and structure it in a way that allows you to try alternative ideas to arrive at a solution. If one idea doesn't work, try another. It often starts with the question 'what if...?'
blocks.title: Key idea

blocks.text: Framing works where there is a clear sense of what needs to be achieved. It means thinking about:

items: how people are going to use the things you plan to make
how you will create value and, critically, for whom

blocks.text: Thinking like a designer means defining clearly the real nature of the underlying problem during exploratory phases. Only once this is agreed does it make sense to move on to alternative solutions.
For each possible solution, a sense check shows how each frame may affect the desired outcome. The UK Design Council formalised this in its 'double diamond' process, with four phases.

blocks.alt: Design Council double diamond: discover, define, develop, deliver, with two diamonds opening and narrowing thinking
blocks.caption: Figure 4 Double Diamond model (Design Council, 2004)

head: Phase
What happens
rows: more insight into the problem or challenge; opens up thinking
focus on specific areas: priorities, test assumptions and feasibility
broaden out again to potential solutions, prototypes and concepts to test
evaluate alternatives to filter down to solutions to finalise and produce

blocks.q: In the double diamond, which phase involves focusing on priorities and testing assumptions and feasibility?
blocks.explain: Define narrows thinking to specific areas, priorities, assumptions and feasibility. Discover and Develop open thinking up; Deliver filters to final solutions.

blocks.q: Which phase broadens thinking to potential solutions, prototypes and concepts?
blocks.explain: Develop opens thinking out again to all potential solutions and prototypes that can be tested.

blocks.text: For more detail see the UK Design Council's double diamond and the Stanford 'd school' (see Further reading in the original course).

blocks.title: Video 5: Brainstorming
blocks.note: A detailed approach to brainstorming: generate as many ideas as you can for a problem or irritation without filtering or judging them.

blocks.title: Activity 4, part 1: Brainstorm
blocks.prompt: Think of a problem or irritation you are aware of, or simply try to create something for fun. Watch the brainstorming video and come up with as many ideas as you can to solve your problem or create something. Try to come up with at least five ideas. Don't filter or judge them in any way yet, and remember they can be anything you want.
blocks.model: A good brainstorm produces at least five varied ideas, written without judging them. Include wild ones too: the next part is where you filter, and the point is to remove early filters like 'that will never work' or 'nobody would go for this' before putting filters back systematically.
points: List at least five ideas
Do not judge or filter ideas yet
Ideas can be anything you want, including wild ones

blocks.title: Try it: Idea lab
blocks.intro: Use the idea lab to push your brainstorm further and generate variations of your ideas before you evaluate them.

blocks.text: Academic Roger Martin and designer Tim Brown (Brown and Martin, 2015) suggest that designers juggle these questions when they assess ideas:

items: **Suitable**: does the idea actually address the issue?
**Feasible**: is it technically possible?
**Acceptable**: is it acceptable to all stakeholders?

blocks.text: Score each idea 1 to 5 for suitability, feasibility and acceptability (5 most, 1 least) and add your own significant criteria, such as fit with family, passion or lifestyle. Then total the scores.

blocks.title: Activity 4, part 2: Score your ideas
blocks.prompt: Using the table above (Table 3 'Will it work?'), write down each idea from your brainstorm and score it 1 to 5 for suitability, feasibility and acceptability, with 5 the most. Add your own filtering criterion (e.g. fit with family, passion, suits lifestyle) and total the scores to see which scores highest. Then reflect: did you want one idea to win?
blocks.model: This is a simple exercise, though oddly effective. Often people feel they want one particular idea to win and 'fix' the scores, or feel disappointed afterwards. This highlights how we tend to filter out ideas 'that will never work' or 'nobody would go for'. It shows the importance of removing those initial filters before putting them back in a systematic way.
points: Scoring ideas against suitable, feasible and acceptable gives a systematic filter
We tend to favour one idea and may 'fix' the scores
Early instinctive filtering ('it will never work') removes ideas too soon
Remove initial filters first, then reintroduce them systematically

blocks.caption: Figure 5 Not all ideas work

blocks.text: It is easy to neglect the value of learning from things that don't work. Most of what we know about entrepreneurs and ideas comes from people who have been successful. Sometimes they were lucky, but more often it was hard work, and learning and recovering from lots of mistakes.
Apple's early handheld touchscreen device, the Newton (1993), was a disastrous mistake. What if the lesson Apple had taken was never to develop another touchscreen mobile device?

One of the key elements of Dyson's story is what he learnt from his ball barrow being stolen. The innovation was to replace the front wheel of a wheelbarrow with a ball, making it much easier to manoeuvre. His idea, however, was stolen by a US company.
This was a valuable lesson in failure to protect his idea, which he later applied to controlling production and intellectual property in future ventures (Blundel et al., 2018, pp. 248-51).

It is easier to learn from your mistakes than to discern the real lessons. People are sensitive to failure and have a real aversion to loss, which can affect your objectivity about whether something will work again. You will often hear 'we tried that before and it didn't work'. Software mantras like 'move fast and break things' or 'fail fast' champion learning from failure.

Learning from and embracing failure can create something stronger, but there can be resistance. Some cultures, countries or organisations do not encourage failure at all, because the risk to reputation or careers is too high.

Failure is not simply inconvenient for some enterprises. The social consequences for social enterprises should not be underestimated or trivialised (UnLtd, 2016). A failed banking app could leave thousands of customers without access to their accounts, unpaid and charged fees through no fault of their own.

Care is needed over *how* you learn from failure: it is the interpretation that matters. Apple did not ditch touchscreens; some suggest the Newton was simply launched before its time, with pricing and handwriting recognition to blame (The Telegraph, 2018).

It is highly likely that one or more aspects of your own idea will be challenged or rejected at some point. You can ignore this feedback, or agree and use it to tweak or revise your idea so it is more robust. Try not to let negative feedback make you falter at the first hurdle.
As you continue, you will see it is not always plain sailing for any entrepreneur, including the four you are following, who will keep sharing their experiences.

blocks.q: The only sensible lesson from an idea that failed is never to try something similar again.
blocks.explain: It is the interpretation that matters. Apple kept developing touchscreens after the Newton; the failure may have been about timing, pricing and handwriting recognition.

blocks.q: What lesson did Dyson draw from his ball barrow idea being stolen by a US company?
options: Protect your idea and control production and intellectual property
blocks.explain: It taught him to protect his ideas and control production and intellectual property in future ventures.

blocks.text: Check what you've learned this session.

blocks.q: According to the definitions used in this course, entrepreneurs are defined by...
options: the size of organisation they work for
their actions: creating or exploiting change for profit, innovating, accepting risk and moving resources
blocks.explain: Entrepreneurs are defined by their actions, not the size of the organisation.

blocks.q: Which of the following are discovery skills? Select all that apply.
blocks.explain: Observing, questioning, curiosity, connectivity, associating and incubation are discovery skills.

blocks.q: Dyson came up with the bagless vacuum cleaner after...
options: a single 'Eureka moment' in the bath
encountering industrial extraction fans and building thousands of prototypes
blocks.explain: He wondered whether industrial extraction technology could work in a domestic setting, then built a few thousand prototypes.

blocks.q: Which Drucker source of innovation is 'changes in society, in perception, mood or meaning'?
blocks.explain: It is an external source.

blocks.q: Evaluating an idea for suitability asks whether it is technically possible.
blocks.explain: That is feasibility. Suitability asks whether the idea actually addresses the issue; acceptability asks whether it is acceptable to all stakeholders.

blocks.q: Alex Bond's team changed from a food label to a spray product mainly because...
options: big food manufacturers found packaging margins too slim to add any label
blocks.explain: The cost of packaging is so slim that any label made it too expensive, so they used the technology for a spray.

blocks.text: Telling a good story, as our entrepreneurs do, is part of turning an idea into reality. You will need to convince others to help, join your team, provide resources or finance, and eventually engage as users or customers.

An entrepreneur is not necessarily the source of innovation. Dyson's first idea of the ball barrow came from frustration; later the ball became part of his vacuum cleaner, though arguably it was the suction that made the difference. Recognising that an industrial approach could be applied to the domestic market, and trying to make it work, was the crucial factor.
In this session you have:

items: heard from entrepreneurs, in particular where their ideas come from
considered how to generate an idea and the tools to evaluate it
listened to examples of ideas that worked and did not, and how they evolved through learning from failure

blocks.text: In the next session you will explore how to make ideas a reality.

chapters.title: Session 2: From idea to reality
chapters.summary: Starting a business: motivation, UK business landscape, growth, protecting IP, business structures and getting support.

blocks.text: Many new businesses fail within two years of starting up, and 50 per cent within three years (Business Wales, 2018). You have considered sources of ideas; but what happens next? This session covers the decisions needed to formally start your business and three vital aspects you must manage simultaneously.

blocks.alt: A woman spinning plates on sticks, facing away from the camera
blocks.caption: Figure 1 Business involves spinning many plates at once

blocks.text: By the end of this session you will be able to:

items: describe your own motivation for starting your enterprise
identify what support and actions you need to make your idea a reality
evaluate alternative business structures to refine those appropriate to your needs

pages.title: Three vital aspects: delivering, running, getting

items: **Delivering the business**: can you consistently meet demand for a product or service others consider worth paying for? If you can't, your business won't get off the ground.

**Running the business**: fulfilling the functions and obligations of an organisation properly, observing the law, and meeting stakeholders' expectations (customers, shareholders, suppliers). Fall foul of the law or let customers down and the business will not last.

**Getting the business**: your ability to find, supply and keep getting new sales, contracts and customers. With no future income you deplete your capital and resources and cannot meet obligations to creditors.

blocks.text: A successful, sustainable business balances and addresses all three aspects at the same time.

blocks.q: Finding, supplying and keeping on getting new sales, contracts and customers is which aspect of business?
blocks.explain: Getting the business is about generating future income streams.

blocks.q: Observing the law and meeting stakeholders' expectations is part of...
blocks.explain: Running the business covers fulfilling the functions and obligations of an organisation properly.

blocks.text: There are a number of considerations when you start: your ambitions for the business, your own motivation, goals, context and circumstances, and the nature of the business you intend to run.

Another important consideration is your **exit strategy**: how you would prefer to leave the business. You may want to be bought out, pass or sell it to family or employees, wind it up, or be taken over. Keep this in mind as you decide what structure your business will take.

What is your motivation? Is this a **lifestyle business**, a way to earn a living that fits your lifestyle using mainly your own skills, talents and/or time? Does it have to fit with a family situation? You may see yourself as self-employed, staying local and small to keep a sensible work-life balance.
Perhaps your business depends on your immediate environment for reasons such as:

items: natural features, like wonderful views, and amenities that you want to exploit
ready access to customers (footfall or easy logistics) or the infrastructure your business needs, from a central location to superfast broadband

blocks.title: Reflection: your motivation
blocks.prompt: Reflect on your own motivation for starting your enterprise, taking into consideration all of the aspects that have so far been discussed.
blocks.model: Your answer is personal. A strong answer says why you want to start (e.g. lifestyle, independence, solving a problem, growth), links this to your skills, family situation, location and resources, and considers how you would eventually exit.
points: State the main reason you want to start the business
Link motivation to lifestyle, skills, family and location
Consider whether you want to stay small or grow
Think about how you might eventually exit

blocks.text: Successive governments have identified low productivity in the UK economy and so have supported entrepreneurship, new business start-ups and therefore new jobs. In 2020 the government estimated around 6 million UK businesses.
Different definitions of small to medium-sized businesses (SMEs) exist, but those used by UK government differentiate on turnover and employee numbers.

items: **Micro-businesses**: fewer than ten employees and turnover under £2m.
**SME**: up to 250 employees and turnover up to £25m. SMEs represent over 99 per cent of all UK businesses (Rhodes, 2017).

blocks.text: UK business angels have continued to invest at a similar level to pre-Covid times (British Business Bank, 2020a). The UK Business Angels Association have continued to prioritise proposals from healthcare; biotech, life sciences and pharmaceuticals; and software as a service.

blocks.alt: Bar chart of small, medium and large enterprises: share of businesses, turnover and employment
blocks.caption: Figure 2 Share of enterprises

blocks.text: The UK government prioritises financial services, science and technology, energy and health. These matter for the security of the economy and are sectors where the UK can be influential. Many more are important, including food and drink, clothing and textiles, and transport. Check the devolved administrations in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, or other countries, to see how emphasis differs.
Government priorities do not stop you building a thriving business in another sector, but funding may be more readily available in priority sectors.

Large companies account for only 0.1 per cent of businesses, but 40 per cent of employment and almost half (49 per cent) of turnover. Growing a small enterprise takes much more than working harder and faster.

blocks.q: Roughly what share of UK businesses are small (0-49 employees)?
blocks.explain: Small businesses are 99.30% of all businesses.

blocks.q: Large companies account for most UK businesses.
blocks.explain: They are only 0.1% of businesses, though they provide 40% of employment and 49% of turnover.

blocks.text: Do you have all the skills, time, resources and organisational ability to keep all three aspects (getting, delivering and running) going? If not, you must consider who will get, do and run your business. That may mean becoming an employer, with all the responsibilities that implies.

Jyoti Banerjee of the M-Institute (a not-for-profit supporting growth of medium-sized businesses) observes that leading a small business versus a medium-sized business is very different and needs quite different behaviours and attitudes.

blocks.title: Video 1: Jyoti Banerjee: mid-sized businesses
blocks.note: Jyoti Banerjee describes how medium-sized businesses are different to small businesses. Small businesses tend to be concerned with survival and viability, and may be based around the owner's lifestyle; a medium-sized business is concerned with growth and scaling up, which needs a different mindset and managerial behaviour.

pages.title: Scaling up to a medium-sized business

blocks.alt: A goldfish jumping from a small fish bowl to a larger one
blocks.caption: Figure 3 Scaling up is one of the biggest challenges for an entrepreneur

blocks.text: Scaling up is arguably one of the biggest challenges for entrepreneurs who have created a successful small business. Being focused on keeping on top of everything, knowing who's doing what, and following every opportunity is very different to deploying a staff of 50 or 200 employees.
As you grow you cannot wrap your arms around it all. Growth means a little less direct control and the ability to find and trust other people to perform their role.

If your idea has high growth potential and you can't finance it yourself, you will need external investment. Growth likely needs employees, a means of production (premises, equipment or people) and a structure, and possibly research and development. All entail increasing costs, and medium-sized businesses can find access to finance harder than larger companies.

Some regulations apply regardless of size. Small businesses may be exempt from some, such as financial audits for turnover below £10.2m and fewer than 50 employees, but medium-sized firms must meet all the requirements of a larger business without its structure and specialist staff.

You must also compete for skilled staff or fund training, pay competitive wages, pensions and benefits, and satisfy investors with a longer term view of how costs can rise while future revenues are generated.
Entrepreneurs who want to run medium-sized businesses have to think differently by setting aside the instinct to do everything themselves because they know they're best at it.

Entrepreneurs must be able and prepared to bring on board a team to spread the load and provide diversity of thinking and new ideas. You will return to financing your business in more detail in Session 7.

blocks.q: Which mindset shift does Banerjee suggest is needed to run a medium-sized business?
options: Bringing on a team and trusting others to share the load
blocks.explain: Entrepreneurs need to set aside the instinct to do everything themselves and bring on a team.

blocks.text: Knowing what you want from setting up your own business is an important early step. This reflection helps you outline your goals and ambitions.

blocks.title: Reflection: your goals
blocks.prompt: Answer these in turn: (1) What does running your own business mean to you? (2) What is your business all about; what is its purpose or mission? (3) Who else will be affected by your decisions? (4) Thinking ahead five years, where do you see yourself, your family, your business? (5) Do you have the mindset Banerjee suggests is vital to grow? (6) What are your personal values? Does your image of the future square with them, and are any likely to conflict?
blocks.model: Five years from now your business could be well established and you could have achieved your goals, but getting there means taking stock of your situation, making decisions and taking action now. A good answer is concrete about purpose, people affected, a five-year picture, readiness to delegate, and any values conflicts.
points: State what running a business means to you and its purpose or mission
Identify others affected (family, employees, customers, community)
Describe where you want yourself, your family and the business in five years
Assess whether you have the growth mindset (delegating, building a team)
Check your personal values against your vision and note conflicts

blocks.text: In Session 1 you explored the business idea. One of the most important decisions in starting your business is how to protect your intellectual property.

**Intellectual property (IP)** is the intangible property that comes from your ideas and thoughts. It includes 'inventions, literary and artistic works, designs, symbols, names and images used in commerce' (WIPO, 2018).
blocks.title: Definition

blocks.text: Protecting your IP makes it much harder for others to steal or copy it, as the Dyson example showed. It has costs, so build them into your growth planning. If you plan to grow by licensing your idea or franchising it, IP is essential.

blocks.alt: Registered trademark, copyright and trademark symbols
blocks.caption: Figure 4 Patent, copyright and trademark symbols

cards.back: Give the inventor the right to prevent others making, using or selling the subject matter under patent. The best protection for a new product.
Covers original works of art, authorship or written copy (books, music, film etc.).
Protect the value of a name, brand, logo or other symbols that distinguish your product, e.g. the Adidas three stripes or the Nike tick.
Allow the owner to take action against anyone who breaches an agreement to keep something confidential, e.g. a family recipe.

blocks.text: Before you register your company and website address, or consider international markets, check whether you can have and use them without infringing another business. Consider cultural references that make your product less attractive overseas.
Also make sure your product and company name work for customers and other stakeholders: is it memorable, and can it be spelled and therefore found?

blocks.q: A family recipe kept confidential and protected by an agreement is best covered by...
blocks.explain: Trade secrets allow the owner to act against anyone who breaches a confidentiality agreement.

blocks.q: Which type of IP protects a brand name or logo?
blocks.explain: Trademarks protect the value of a name, brand, logo or symbol.

blocks.text: This course cannot give everything you need on IP, but here are tips to discuss with a legal adviser:

items: If you work for someone else, check your employment terms so your employer doesn't own new ideas or inventions. Don't work on your idea in their time with their resources; keep employed work and new venture distinct.
A non-disclosure or confidentiality agreement lets you talk to experts and advisers without jeopardising your position.
Conversations with friends and colleagues may produce joint ideas or loose proposals to be co-founders. Once agreed, agree the terms of the relationship.

If working with others (e.g. independent contractors), ensure all IP rights are assigned to your company. If you employ someone from a competitor, check they aren't bound by confidentiality or non-compete conditions.
If you use open source software, check the rights and permissions. If you use images on your website, don't infringe others' copyright.
Protection should cover all the country markets you intend to trade in.

blocks.text: While this course is written as if starting a business is linear, in reality you operate on many fronts at the same time.

blocks.title: Activity 1: Finding advice
blocks.prompt: Make notes on whether you need to get advice on protecting your idea. Lots of information is available online, and your local enterprise partnership or economic development agency will often have local law firms that provide seminars and free advice for new businesses. Useful websites on starting a business: GOV.UK, Forbes, TechCrunch.
blocks.model: If you have a novel concept, product or idea and have invested a lot of time and energy in it, it makes no sense to let someone else capitalise on it. Seeking professional advice early may save you a lot of trouble later, or costly challenges from employers, employees or colleagues.
points: Consider which kind of IP (patent, copyright, trademark, trade secret) applies to your idea
Seek professional advice early to avoid later costly disputes
Check employer ownership of ideas and use confidentiality agreements
Use free sources such as GOV.UK and local enterprise agencies

pages.title: What kind of business structures are there?

blocks.text: One of the early decisions is what legal structure your business will take. Distinguish the **legal form** (how the law regards the enterprise) from the **organisational type** (how you regard and present it). You can have several organisational types but only one legal form.

head: Structure
Key points
rows: Simplest way to operate; personal liability for debts and tax; not separate from the operation
Two or more co-owners share the income; business not separate from its operators
At least one general and one limited partner (not both); limited partners liable up to their contribution and cannot manage

head: Structure
Key points
rows: Separate from its operators; finances separate from owner's; can retain profits after corporation tax; needs directors, shares, memorandum and articles; registered with Companies House
Franchisor gives a franchisee the right to use its name, logo and business model (e.g. McDonalds, Subway); a way to start with less new-business activity, or to scale your idea

blocks.q: Which structure treats the business as separate from its operators and requires registration with Companies House?
blocks.explain: A limited company is a separate legal entity with its own finances and must be registered with Companies House (UK).

blocks.text: There are common organisational types used by social businesses:

items: **Social enterprise**: primarily social objectives; profit mostly reinvested in the business or community rather than maximising shareholder profit.
**Community enterprise**: a social enterprise owned and run by a geographical community or community of interest.

**Co-operative**: an autonomous association of persons united voluntarily to meet common economic, social and cultural needs through a jointly-owned, democratically controlled enterprise (International Co-operative Alliance).

pages.title: Types of co-operative and other social forms

items: **Worker co-operative**: owned and run by its workers
**Housing co-operative**: owned and run by its tenants
**Consumer co-operative**: owned and run by its customers
**Co-operative consortium**: owned and run by other businesses that use its services
**Multi-stakeholder co-operative**: a mixture of any or all of the above

cards.back: An organisation created to hold land as an asset for community use.
A non-profit financial institution owned and operated entirely by its members.
A community-based enterprise that secures and manages community assets.
A business committed to creating employment and training for people furthest from the labour market.

pages.title: Ethical business and choosing a structure

blocks.text: Any of these types can also be an ethical business. A social enterprise is established to benefit people and the planet as its primary purpose; an ethical business seeks to minimise harm to people and the planet.

Deciding on structure requires thinking about how you will finance the business and its anticipated size. An individual can trade for a social purpose as well as being a sole trader and call themselves a social business: there is very little regulation of organisational types in branding or marketing.
Refer back to your goals. Structure has implications for who controls the business and whether audited accounts and named directors are required.

Funding has become available to support a range of 'not-for-profit' enterprises: community companies, social enterprises, charities and community interest companies. They are increasingly important as central government devolves local service provision and funding cuts reduce services.

Setting one up means considering the same things as any for-profit enterprise: demand, financial viability, skills and capacity, and securing funding. But as these are often publicly regulated bodies, they have a more complex legal structure, so contact one of the organisations listed at the end of the session.
Do some research of your own before deciding. These questions help narrow the options for discussion with a professional adviser (GOV.UK is a good place to start):

items: Starting alone or with others? What if one wants to leave, retire or move away?
Taking over a business from someone else? What is its structure, who owns it, what involvement might they want?
How much administration? Some structures don't require registering, incorporating, filing or auditing accounts, or annual returns.
How much finance, and from where? What assets could be collateral? How do shareholders affect your growth plan?
Tax advantages or protection of personal assets?
Other considerations like community, surroundings or the environment?

pages.title: Activity 2: Deciding on the structure of your business

head: Structure
How would this work for me?
What wouldn't work for me?

blocks.title: Activity 2: Deciding on the structure
blocks.prompt: Using your answers to the questions above, look up the types of structure that exist to see how they would fit for you. For each of sole trader, partnership, limited liability partnership, limited company, social business and franchise, note how it would work for you and what wouldn't work for you.
blocks.model: It is impossible to give general feedback without knowing you, your circumstances and your idea. You will get a lot more from a discussion with a legal adviser if you have done preparatory thinking and are clear about what matters to you: your goals, future ambitions, lifestyle and whether and how you want to grow.
points: Compare each structure against your own goals and circumstances
Consider liability, finance, control, administration and tax
Note which structures suit staying small and which suit growth
Prepare questions for a professional adviser

blocks.text: What are the core functions and roles that keep a business running? At this point it is interesting to see how our entrepreneurs started out.

blocks.title: Video 2: Starting out
blocks.note: The entrepreneurs describe their first steps. Emma Prince talked to local schools and the council (who all said there was a shortage), gave three months' notice to network and learn pitfalls from charities, and was supported by her family. Claudio Marturano wanted out of the corporate world, got advice from the Open University, Business Gateway and Scottish Enterprise, then took the plunge. Alex Bond and colleagues sought a patent first, then joined an Imperial College accelerator that taught them about forming a company, raising funds and market research. Nick Allen found a former M&S buyer to help shape the brand, then used local growth hubs, the Department for International Trade and trading standards for advice.

blocks.text: **Bootstrapping**: many small businesses start small, with no external help or funding. They try to turn their hand to everything, which can mean long hours, learning new skills and relying on a lot of advice. Don't panic!

A dilemma is when to hire the first employees. Being a good employer means taking responsibility on a number of fronts. Consider the economics term **opportunity cost**: at some point consider whether it is cheaper or more efficient for someone else to carry out functions (running, getting or delivering the business).

If you can make more profit per hour turning out something to sell than doing your book-keeping, it makes economic sense to hire someone to do the books. This 'make or buy' decision applies to each aspect of your business. Reflect on Jyoti Banerjee's points in Section 3.

pages.title: Activity 3: Core functions of a business

blocks.title: Activity 3: Core functions of a business
blocks.prompt: Under each of these three headings, make a list of tasks and roles you would need to consider when running your business: Finance; Administration and governance; Sales, marketing and customer service.
blocks.model: Finance: book-keeping; banking cash and cheques; payroll; invoicing; chasing unpaid invoices; VAT returns; budgeting; forecasting cash flow; settling invoices. Administration and governance: statutory returns; customer records; supplier and employee contracts; pensions; data protection and security; leases and hire contracts; insurances; share and partnership agreements; managing stock; securing premises; policies (refunds, payment terms, loyalty, employment terms). Sales, marketing and customer service: getting and converting leads; answering enquiries; following up leads; closing deals; responding to tenders; drafting proposals; solving customer queries such as complaints and payment errors; replacing and refunding goods.
points: Finance: book-keeping, payroll, invoicing, VAT, budgeting, cash-flow forecasting
Administration and governance: statutory returns, contracts, insurance, data protection, policies
Sales, marketing and customer service: leads, enquiries, closing deals, tenders, complaints
Consider which tasks you can do and which to hire or buy in

pages.title: Developing your enterprise and finding help

blocks.text: There is a lot to running a successful business. If you don't have the skills now, you can acquire them over time; many free courses on book-keeping, budgeting and marketing exist on OpenLearn and the internet.

Friends, family or your extended network may offer support. Working with people you know and trust may seem obvious, but think it through. They have your best interests at heart but also their own priorities, jobs and responsibilities.

items: Can you ensure their investment or support is sustainable and won't lead to unacceptable risk or loss for them?
Will you be able to pay them?
Will the business sustain all your needs and ambitions?
Will relationships withstand disagreements, advice that goes wrong, mistakes, long hours and other pressures?
Would two people earning from the same business be an advantage or a pressure?

pages.title: Reflection: working with people you trust

blocks.title: Reflection: the pros of working with people you trust
blocks.prompt: Many family businesses work very well. So far there have been more cons than pros. Find a counterbalance: what are the advantages of working with people you trust and who may share your ambition?
blocks.model: Advantages include trust and loyalty, shared commitment and ambition, flexibility on hours and pay in the early days, quick and candid communication, shared values, and a ready-made support network that can share the load and bring different skills.
points: Trust and loyalty reduce risk in the early days
Shared ambition and commitment
Flexibility and willingness to share the workload
Complementary skills and a ready-made support network

blocks.text: Public bodies provide support, resources, information and advice, and can signpost local organisations. Here are starting points in the UK nations and Ireland.

items: England and UK-wide: Entrepreneur Handbook (grants and funding), Local Enterprise Partnership network (growth hubs), Social Enterprise UK

Scotland: Business Gateway, Highlands and Islands Enterprise, Highlands and Islands Social Enterprise Zone, Just Enterprise, Scottish Institute for Enterprise, Scottish Enterprise, Scottish Government Rural Business Support, Scottish Rural Network
Northern Ireland and Ireland: Enterprise Northern Ireland, Invest Northern Ireland, Social Entrepreneurs Ireland, Social Enterprise Northern Ireland
Wales: Business Wales, Wales Council for Voluntary Action, Trade & Invest Wales

blocks.title: Activity 4: Finding useful resources
blocks.prompt: Make a note of, or bookmark, the organisations above that may be most useful to you so you can come back to them throughout the course as you develop your business. Write which ones you chose and why.
blocks.model: Pick the national and local bodies relevant to where you live and your sector, and say what each offers (grants, advice, networking, mentoring, training).
points: Choose organisations relevant to your nation and sector
Note what each offers (funding, advice, networks, training)
Include at least one local source of support

blocks.q: What are the three vital aspects of a business to manage simultaneously?
options: Delivering, running and getting the business
blocks.explain: Delivering, running and getting the business.

blocks.q: A sole trader's business is legally separate from the owner.
blocks.explain: Sole traders are not separate from the operation; they are personally liable for debts and tax.

blocks.q: The 'make or buy' decision about hiring someone to do book-keeping is based on which economic idea?
blocks.explain: If you earn more per hour producing than doing the books, it makes economic sense to hire someone else.

blocks.q: Which structures involve co-owners where in law the business is not separate from its operators? Select all that apply.
blocks.explain: Sole traders and (ordinary) partnerships are not separate legal entities; a limited company is.

blocks.q: A franchisor gives a franchisee the right to use...
options: their business name, logo and business model
blocks.explain: A franchise is one way to start a business with less new-business activity, or to scale an idea.

blocks.q: Medium-sized businesses can find access to finance harder than larger companies.
blocks.explain: Medium-sized businesses must find and manage access to finance to grow, and this can be more difficult than for larger companies.

blocks.text: Professional advisers, lawyers and accountants, can advise and set up your company for a fee, but do your research first and take advantage of the many public bodies that support new and growing businesses. They offer networks, gatherings where you meet other local businesses (a source of custom and advice), training, templates and guidelines, and may provide a mentor or personal adviser.
In this session you have:

items: recognised how businesses are sustainable by managing all the core functions of getting, doing and running the business
identified several different types of business entity depending on how big the business may become
considered how your motivation and financing affect your business structure
learned how to assess gaps in the core skills your business needs
seen how important professional advice and support from others is

blocks.text: In the next session you will explore how your business can create value, using the business model canvas.

chapters.title: Session 3: Creating value
chapters.summary: Use the business model canvas to describe how your business creates and delivers value, and learn the dilemmas every entrepreneur faces, including when to pivot.

pages.title: A business is a value delivery system

blocks.text: A business is a value delivery system.

It is only by creating something that people are willing to pay for or support that you will make money and be able to sustain your enterprise. Value goes beyond cost or price: sentimental value has nothing to do with money, and the premium we pay for an exclusive brand goes beyond the cost of materials, production and delivery.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

items: create and describe your business model as a foundation for creating value
identify the kind of dilemmas that entrepreneurs face in setting up their business
recognise why it is important to remain flexible and willing to adapt and change to be successful.

blocks.text: It is tempting to skip theory and go straight to creating your product or service. But without a clear legal status and business model you may quickly run into problems with cash-flow, HMRC, suppliers and customers. A little planning now helps others see how to set things up well and who they are dealing with.
In Session 2 you looked at the three essential activities of managing a business:

items: **Running** the business: the 'must do' activities such as invoicing, paying tax and complying with regulations
**Getting** the business: finding, attracting and keeping customers
**Delivering** the business: creating the product or service customers want to use or buy.

blocks.text: The models in this course work as a checklist or framework: you can quickly build a visual outline of your business to develop it and to explain it to people who can support you.
The traditional approach to a business can be represented as a simple left-to-right system: create the product, make the product, then sell the product.

blocks.alt: Three arrows in a row reading Create the product, Make the product, Sell the product.
blocks.caption: Figure 1 Traditional product-oriented system

blocks.text: McKinsey's value delivery system offers an alternative, but still quite traditional, view. It starts from the customer's value rather than from the product.

blocks.alt: Three arrows: Choose the value (understand value drivers, select target, define benefits and price), Provide the value (product, process, design, procurement, manufacturing, distribution, service, price), Communicate the value to the customer (sales message, advertising, promotion, public relations).
blocks.caption: Figure 2 McKinsey's value delivery system

blocks.text: In both systems the assumption is that as you move from left to right, there are opportunities to create value.

blocks.title: Business model canvas
blocks.text: Sometimes called the 'value nine box model', proposed by Alex Osterwalder (Osterwalder and Pigneur, 2010). It is a systematic way of working through the essential elements of any business.

The nine boxes are not seen in isolation but as an integrated way of operating, with each part capable of adding value. The canvas has become very popular amongst the start-up community, especially technology-based start-ups.

As you work through the course, use it to capture ideas and experiment with your own version as each of the nine aspects of the business model is discussed. The next pages let you build your own canvas in the app.
First watch the short video, which defines a number of terms and brings the business model canvas to life. Then tap each definition and choose the matching term from the nine boxes.

blocks.title: Video 1 The business model canvas
blocks.note: A short video defining the terms of the business model canvas.

blocks.title: Activity 1: match each definition to its term

pairs.def: The bundles of products and services designed to appeal to and provide value to different customer segments
The groups of people with a distinct need or use for your products or services
What assets (people, equipment, premises) are absolutely necessary to deliver value
People or organisations with expertise or the ability to do essential things you rely upon but cannot do cost effectively yourself
How you will relate to your customers (loyalty schemes, discounts, rewards, recognition of greatest need)
What things you absolutely need to do very well
Where costs arise in the business
The touchpoints: places or means of distributing your product or service
How and through which activities you will capture value

blocks.title: Try it: Business Model Canvas
blocks.intro: Fill in the nine boxes for your own idea. Leave gaps where you do not yet know: those are the areas to investigate as the course goes on.

blocks.text: As you work through this course you will cover all aspects of the business model canvas. You will have more detail or ideas for some parts and less for others. Activity 2 helps you identify these areas.

blocks.title: Activity 2 Thinking of your own business model canvas
blocks.prompt: Take a few minutes to think about your own business idea and what aspects of a business model you could clearly describe for it now. Which will you need to work on? Note your thoughts down.
blocks.hint: Go through the nine boxes one by one: which can you fill in confidently, and which are still blank?
blocks.model: Answers are personal. A good response names the canvas boxes you can already describe (for example customer segments or the value proposition) and identifies the ones that still need research (for example key partners, channels or cost structure), with a note of how you might find out.
points: Identify the canvas boxes you can already describe clearly
Identify the boxes where you have gaps or only assumptions
Say what you could do to fill the gaps, e.g. research competitors or talk to customers

blocks.text: Your business model should be unique to your idea, so you are the expert in it. While you may share component parts with other businesses, your model differentiates you. Competitive advantage, and a compelling reason for customers to favour you, can come from any part of the model, including your pricing strategy and the elements of your value proposition.

blocks.title: Video 2 Plan or jump in?
blocks.note: Our entrepreneurs talk about their business model and whether they planned it or whether it emerged over time.

blocks.title: Example: SAGA
blocks.text: SAGA targeted a very specific group, the over 50s. Founded by Sidney De Haan in 1959, it began with packaged holidays, then added travel, caravan and motor insurance, financial services and latterly health care. It owns a direct mail and fulfilment service and a subscription magazine read by around one million readers. Think about how you will reach your own customers.

For each part of your business model there are choices, and it can be hard to decide what is best. As a new venture you may have no previous experience, or no predecessors to learn from. That is quite normal: every entrepreneur and start-up faces dilemmas about what to do.
Dilemma 1: building confidence

So much is unknown and untested, yet supporters, investors and customers are likely to need more certainty, especially for a new or unique idea. Passion, self-belief, hard work and persistence matter, but a lack of evidence may deter important stakeholders. You will have to convince stakeholders even before you convince customers.

items: Planning how you will operate lets you sense check your idea with others and reduces the risk of being blinded by your own enthusiasm.
An accountant can sense check your assumptions about costs and revenue streams.
Basic market research and researching competitor offers give evidence and comfort to stakeholders.

blocks.text: It is very common for start-ups to 'bootstrap': to operate with no external help or finance beyond one's own savings or personal credit (first discussed in Session 2). Keeping it all under your own control can be exhilarating, but pretty soon it may prove overwhelming or even counter-productive.

blocks.title: Activity 3 Limitations of bootstrapping
blocks.prompt: Can you think of three signs that indicate it is time to go beyond bootstrapping to seek external resources?
blocks.hint: Think about workload, money and skills.
blocks.model: Possible signs: you are overwhelmed and cannot keep up with demand on your own; you lack the skills or knowledge for key tasks such as accounting, marketing or technical work; your own savings or credit cannot fund the growth the business needs; growth is being held back by space or equipment; you are missing opportunities because you cannot invest.
points: The workload has become overwhelming or counter-productive for one person
You lack key skills or knowledge that others could supply
Your own savings or credit cannot fund further growth
Demand or opportunities are outgrowing your resources

blocks.text: The mix of knowledge, skills and 'personality' of you, your staff, volunteers or network is unique and can be part of your competitive advantage. Many small firms do not employ support staff, using technology (e.g. accounting software) or outsourcing (e.g. a virtual PA, customer service centre or sales) instead.

Your idea may need premises and employees from the outset, but for many start-ups growth is gradual until they outgrow their own resources. Entrepreneurs are known for 'paying it forward': giving others the help, advice and support they once received.

blocks.title: Incubators
blocks.text: Typically physical work spaces, which may also provide training, mentors, access to commercial networks and equipment. They may be rent free or charge rent or a membership fee, often have a sector focus (e.g. biotech) and are often aligned with universities or enterprise development agencies.

blocks.title: Accelerators
blocks.text: A more recent concept based on the original 'Y Combinator', a US programme that began in 2005 to support digital start-ups.

blocks.title: Video 3 What are accelerators?
blocks.note: Describes a range of accelerators run by Barclays, Lloyds of London and Microsoft, based in London.

blocks.text: This model of support has been replicated all over the world. As well as development support, accelerators focus on investment and the potential for high growth, so they are more selective and take start-ups on in cohorts to develop business plans, prototypes and a pitch to investors. Programmes last from three to 12 months. Investors usually seek equity rather than a fee, and there may be mentorship, training and seed funding (the initial investment). Some provide workspace, others services only.

blocks.alt: Two maps of the UK showing the locations of incubators (left, purple markers) and accelerators (right, blue markers), concentrated in England and especially the south-east.
blocks.caption: Figure 3 Location of accelerators and incubators in the UK (NESTA, 2018)

blocks.text: **Co-working spaces** simply provide a place to work in contact with other companies or organisations (some are run as social enterprises), plus access to networks, events and publicity opportunities.
To improve is to change; to be perfect is to change often.

blocks.title: Pivot
blocks.text: To make a change in your strategy without changing your vision. Eric Ries (2011), known for the 'lean start-up' methodology, is credited with the term.

Pivoting is a key decision point when something isn't working, or isn't working the way you thought. It means finding ways around obstacles to achieve your ultimate goal by solving a customer problem or meeting a need. Ries advocates developing your business by testing and learning from both successes and failures.

The classic dilemma is knowing when to stop doing something, when to stick with it and when to do it differently. Giving up can be painful if you have invested a lot of emotion and belief, especially if you are taking over someone else's ideas.
Customer segment pivot
You develop a product with teenagers in mind but, through time and testing, recognise it has more potential for adults. If you then target and design around adults, this is a customer segment pivot.
Need or problem pivot

You believe your idea meets one problem, but find the product is doing something more compelling for those customers. PayPal was originally intended to be cybersecurity software but, after a reported five pivots, became a secure payment system for mobile and online use, and a beneficiary of the explosion in e-commerce.
Most, if not all, successful companies have had to consider when and how to change: to take advantage of opportunities, to learn from customer feedback and behaviour, or to avoid failure.

blocks.q: Which statement best describes the business model canvas?
options: A legal document that registers your business
A visual way of working through nine integrated elements of a business, each able to add value
A forecast of profit and loss for the first year
A list of competitors in your market
blocks.explain: The canvas (Osterwalder and Pigneur, 2010) is a systematic, integrated way of describing the essential elements of a business in nine boxes.

blocks.q: Which canvas element describes the touchpoints, i.e. places or means of distributing your product or service?
blocks.explain: Channels are the touchpoints through which you reach customers and distribute your offering.

blocks.q: The traditional product-oriented system moves from selling the product to creating the product.
blocks.explain: It runs left to right: create the product, make the product, then sell the product.

blocks.q: A founder who has run everything alone from personal savings is now overwhelmed by the workload. Which dilemma are they facing?
blocks.explain: Bootstrapping can become overwhelming or counter-productive, which is a sign to seek external resources.

blocks.q: Which of these is typically true of accelerators, in contrast with incubators?
options: They focus on investment and high growth, take cohorts for 3 to 12 months and often seek equity
They are only for social enterprises
blocks.explain: Accelerators are more selective, run cohort programmes of between three and 12 months, and investors usually take equity rather than a fee.

blocks.q: Which of these is an example of a pivot?
options: Changing your strategy while keeping your vision, e.g. targeting adults instead of teenagers
Refusing to change because of earlier investment
blocks.explain: To pivot is to change your strategy without changing your vision, learning from testing and customer feedback.

blocks.text: In this session you have:

items: considered different ways of looking at the business model to deliver value to customers
familiarised yourself with the business model canvas, a visual summary of how you will realise your business idea
recognised how the canvas makes clear who the business is aimed at, its infrastructure, key resources and activities
identified how your business model is unique to you and that every element offers opportunities to innovate
considered how your business is likely to change as you test and learn from customers and gain experience.

blocks.text: You also explored dilemmas entrepreneurs face: building confidence, managed growth, finding support and pivoting. Keep checking back and adapting your own canvas, highlighting gaps to investigate and using your learning to prepare an action plan. In Session 4 you zoom in on your customers and the market for your product.

chapters.title: Session 4: Customers and markets
chapters.summary: Identify who your customers are, understand the market you compete in and decide how you will compete, ending with the 15-question badge quiz.

blocks.text: Who is going to buy your offering and why should they? Customers, markets and competitors together are the domain of marketing. To paraphrase Peter Drucker, any enterprise is a mix of innovation and marketing.

This means addressing questions that arose in your business model in Session 3: who is going to buy this? How do I communicate the benefits? How much will they pay? Marketing for an established business (maintaining market share, launching new products) is quite different from marketing for a new business.
By the end of this session you will be able to:

items: identify the customers that your business is aimed at
describe in detail the market you are competing in
define who you think you will be competing with.

blocks.text: Who are my customers? It seems simple, but the first question is: are they customers at all?

items: **Customers** purchase a good or service. Buying a box of avocadoes for your 'pop up' café makes you a customer, but not a consumer.
**Consumers** use a product or service. If stationery is bought centrally in a large organisation, you are a consumer but not the buying customer. If you choose it yourself, you may be both.

**Client** is often used in professional services such as accountancy, and increasingly in the public and third sector, because it suggests a mutual expectation and a stake each side has in the relationship.

blocks.title: Activity 1 (part 1) Customer, consumer or client
blocks.prompt: How do you think of your customers? Are they buyers or users? Would it be accurate to think of them as customers, consumers or clients? Or is there another way that you think of them?
blocks.hint: Who pays, and who actually uses the product or service?
blocks.model: The answer depends on your idea. A strong answer separates who buys from who uses (they may differ, e.g. a parent buys and a child uses, or an employer buys and staff use), says which of customer, consumer or client fits, and notes if a different word such as member or user better describes the relationship.
points: Distinguish buyers (customers) from users (consumers)
Say whether 'client' fits, i.e. a professional or mutual relationship
Note where the buyer and the user are different people
Choose the term that best reflects the relationship you want

blocks.text: In Video 1 all of our entrepreneurs refer to customers. Watch the video, paying particular attention to how they describe them.

blocks.title: Video 1 Who are your customers?
blocks.note: Claudio, Alex, Emma and Nick describe their customers.

blocks.title: Activity 1 (part 2) Your target audience
blocks.prompt: Having listened to Claudio, Alex, Emma and Nick, make some notes for yourself about how you might describe the target audience for your marketing communications, products and services.
blocks.hint: Who are they, where are they, and what do they need?
blocks.model: A good description names the specific group you are aiming at (not 'everyone'), where they are, what need or problem they have, and how you will reach them. It may also distinguish buyers from users, and note other people who must be persuaded such as suppliers or funders.
points: Describe a specific target group rather than everyone
Say where they are and what they need or want
Distinguish buyers from users where they differ
Consider how you will reach and communicate with them

blocks.text: Usually we are both customer and consumer: we buy food so that we can eat it. Here 'customer' means the relationship between your business and the people you want to engage through your offer. Previously, organisations developed products and you paid for them: a transactional relationship. Recently there has been a shift towards customer relationships, loyalty and engagement, with companies engaging customers as advocates for their business.

blocks.alt: A personal trainer coaching a client through a barbell lift in a gym.
blocks.caption: Figure 1 Personal trainer and client relationship

blocks.text: Customers are stakeholders, and may be involved in value creation: for a personal trainer, customer value includes their own effort as much as yours.

Ideas often arise from being close to a product or service and the person who might use it. The source of your idea might be your experience as a disgruntled customer who spotted something others missed. That insight is something larger organisations may lack, and can be a source of competitive advantage.
But are you typical?

Can you be sure you represent the customers you target? Are there others like you, and how many? You can only answer by engaging with potential customers. Even before you know your offer, you need to pass it by other people: family, sympathetic suppliers who might offer good credit terms, banks and other investors.

blocks.title: Internal communication or marketing
blocks.text: Suppliers, distributors and funders must trust your judgement, feel your experience is authentic and believe you are reliable. You need to persuade these people just as much as your customers.
Now listen to our four entrepreneurs describe how they have used feedback and input from customers to shape their businesses.

blocks.title: Video 2 Using customer feedback
blocks.note: Four entrepreneurs describe how customer feedback and input shaped their businesses.

blocks.text: When watching you might have noted the different ways the entrepreneurs talked about different stakeholders, and perhaps even some tentativeness about knowing who their customers are.
