When starting up, widen the range of potential customers you speak to for a better sense of the market, even without a prototype. Market researchers run **focus groups**: facilitated group discussions that gather qualitative feedback and, if well moderated, help you understand issues at a deeper level.

Facilitators ask questions, show or demonstrate products, use images or share concepts and key messages. They record how the group responds, positively and negatively, whether views are held by all or some, and the reasons behind them.

blocks.title: Share early and often
blocks.text: This idea, common in the software industry, is how many companies operate. Lego is well known for involving its broad customer and fan base in developing and designing products. Could you use that approach, or at least adopt a similar ethos?

pages.title: Activity 2: testing with a focus group

blocks.text: Imagine you ran one focus group of people you know, with positive results. Now you arrange a second with a broader range of 'real' or potential customers, some with no obvious interest in your offer. Market researchers ask (adapted from Kotler et al., 2012):

items: Are the benefits clearly communicated and believable?
Does it address a need or solve a problem?
What other products or services could meet the need?
How valuable would customers perceive it to be?
Would they use or purchase it?
How often, and where would they look for it?

blocks.title: Activity 2 Testing and learning from feedback
blocks.prompt:
Try three thought experiments:
1. Think about how you would answer the questions above for your own idea and note your answers.
2. The first focus group were people you know, or who know you. How are the people in the second group the same or different in views, experiences and feedback?
3. Draft how you might run or structure a focus group to elicit a response to these questions. What questions might you ask? What would you probe? Are there images, products, assumptions or scenarios you would test?
blocks.hint: You cannot get meaningful responses from others until you have thought the questions through yourself.
blocks.model: Your own answers should cover benefits, the need met, alternatives, perceived value, likelihood and frequency of purchase. The second group will probably be less biased and more critical, less polite, with different experiences and less knowledge of you, so their feedback is more honest and may reveal doubts or segments you had not considered. A focus group plan has a clear structure: a welcome and ground rules, open questions on needs, a demonstration or concept shown, questions on the six points, probing of reasons, and recording of who thinks what.
points: Answer the market researchers' questions for your own idea first
Friends and family tend to be supportive; strangers are more honest and varied
Plan open questions and what you want to probe, not just yes or no questions
Decide what to show or test, such as images, a prototype or scenarios
Record whether views are held by all or only some, and why

blocks.text: Working through the focus group activity starts to sense check and refine the value you create for the customer. Thinking about your 'usual suspect' touches on who your ideal customer is, and asks you to think about intended and perhaps even unintended customers.

blocks.title: Persona
blocks.text: A detailed description, often based on real information, of a perfect or even difficult customer. Personas are folded into the development process and inform decisions about how different groups might be treated. User Experience Development emerged in the software industry and is increasingly common across services.
On the next page you can build a persona for your own customer.

blocks.title: Try it: Customer persona
blocks.intro: Describe a typical customer for your idea in detail: who they are, what they need and where you can reach them. Revisit it as you learn more.

blocks.text: Customers come in all forms, and different customers help you create value in different ways. This matters as you grow, especially in listening to the 'right customers'. Reinartz and Kumar (2002) suggested four customer segments, shown by profitability and by short-term or long-term relationship.

blocks.alt: A two by two matrix of profitability (high or low) against short-term or long-term customers, giving Butterflies, True friends, Strangers and Barnacles, each with actions.
blocks.caption: Figure 2 The Loyalty Model (The Open University, 2018)

head: Segment
Fit and profit
What to do
rows: Good fit between offer and needs; high profit potential
Aim for transactional satisfaction, not attitudinal loyalty. Milk the accounts only as long as they are active. Challenge: cease investing soon enough.
Communicate consistently but not too often. Build both attitudinal and behavioural loyalty. Delight them to nurture, defend and retain.
Make no investment in these relationships. Make profit on every transaction.
Measure both the size and share of wallet. If share is small, focus on up- and cross-selling. If the size of wallet is small, impose strict cost controls.

blocks.text: In an ideal world customers would find your offer valuable, buy it, tell their friends and buy every day regardless of cost. That is unlikely. What they tell you about the market and competition may provide the vital information that leads to a pivot (Session 3).

A standard way to think about your offering is the four, now seven, Ps that make up the **marketing mix**: product, price, place, promotion, plus people, process and physical evidence, all aimed at the target market.

blocks.alt: Diagram with Product, Physical evidence, Place, Process, People, Price and Promotion each pointing to a central box labelled Target market.
blocks.caption: Figure 3 The seven Ps which make up the marketing mix

blocks.text: Given the focus on customers in this session, try replacing the four Ps with a more customer-oriented version.

blocks.title: Activity 3 (part 1) Which P corresponds to which C?
blocks.prompt: Match each of the four Ps (Price, Promotion, Place, Product) to one of the four Cs: Cost, Communication, Convenience, Customer needs/wants.
blocks.hint: Ask what each P looks like from the customer's side.
blocks.model: Product matches Customer needs/wants; Price matches Cost; Place matches Convenience; Promotion matches Communication.
points: Product corresponds to customer needs and wants
Price corresponds to cost (to the customer)
Place corresponds to convenience
Promotion corresponds to communication

blocks.title: Activity 3 (part 2) The point of the four Cs
blocks.prompt: What do you think is the point of identifying the four Cs?
blocks.hint: Whose perspective does each set of letters take?
blocks.model: The four Cs shift the viewpoint from what the business does (the Ps) to what the customer experiences. They keep you focused on customer needs, the real cost to them, how convenient it is to buy, and two-way communication rather than one-way promotion, which helps ensure the offer creates value for the customer.
points: The Ps are business-centred; the Cs take the customer's viewpoint
It keeps focus on customer needs and the total cost to the customer
It reminds you to consider convenience and communication, not just selling
This helps check that the offer really creates value for customers

pages.title: What does the market look like?

blocks.text: Perhaps the simplest way to categorise markets is business to business (B2B) or consumer facing (B2C, business to consumer). Within these, consider (adapted from The Open University, 2012):

items: **Geography:** where is it located? Local or international?
**Demographics:** size of other businesses in it, stage of maturity, volume of potential business
**Behavioural characteristics:** how do businesses compete? Value of purchases, frequency (one-off or regular)
**Decision-making process:** who makes the purchase decision, what or who influences them, and what do we know about them?

blocks.text: These shape your understanding of the market and help you refine your offer and the segments to focus on.

Shifts in geography, behaviour, competition and customers can create opportunities. Ten years ago you would probably have bought a mattress from a shop: it is expensive, infrequent and you want to try before you buy. Now some companies sell direct online, offering an extended home trial: literally the opportunity to 'sleep on it'.

blocks.alt: Screenshot of the Leesa mattress website: 'A Better Place to Sleep', with four reasons to choose Leesa including easier shopping and a 100-night risk-free trial.
blocks.caption: Figure 4 Buying a mattress online (Leesa Sleep, 2018)

blocks.title: Reflect: the move online
blocks.prompt: Reflect on the trend of moving purchases online to a direct-to-consumer model, supported by social media and by the need to provide certain guarantees. Convenience is clearly an important factor. Why might that be? As a secondary thought, what opportunities have arisen for businesses providing warehousing, couriers, delivery and packaging, and social media advertising?
blocks.hint: Think about what customers avoid, and who else benefits.
blocks.model: Convenience matters because customers save time and effort (no travel, no awkward showrooms), can compare easily and, with free trials and guarantees, the risk of buying online is reduced. The shift has created opportunities for warehousing, couriers, delivery and packaging solutions and social media advertising providers, which is changing the nature of the customer relationship.
points: Online direct buying saves customers time and effort
Trials and guarantees reduce the risk of buying without trying
Social media helps reach and persuade customers directly
New opportunities for warehousing, couriers, packaging and social media advertising

blocks.text: Markets have a lifecycle: they grow, mature and often disappear, and each phase has a different character (adapted from Kotler et al., 2012).

head: Phase
What happens
rows: Sales are small; often difficult to make a profit because of the costs of taking the offer to market
Market grows rapidly, giving opportunities for profit; others may enter
Sales growth tails away then plateaus; profits still present but competition may be intense

blocks.text: The model shows how competition and profit vary by stage, and asks questions about organisational strategy.

blocks.alt: Bell-shaped curve of new customers over time (innovators 2.5%, early adopters 13.5%, early majority 34%, late majority 34%, laggards 16%) with a rising S-shaped cumulative market share curve.
blocks.caption: Figure 5 Rogers' technology adoption curve

blocks.text: The bell-shaped curve shows when successive customer groups enter the market; the steep rising curve shows cumulative market share, ending in saturation. Rogers (1962) focuses on the consumer rather than the product lifecycle. Early adopters are typically well educated with higher disposable income. He also described phases to move consumers along: Awareness, Persuasion, Trialling, Adoption and Consolidation.
The lifecycle model has a product focus. It may also help to ask the same questions of the technology adoption curve.

blocks.title: Activity 4 The product life cycle
blocks.prompt:
1. How well does the lifecycle model apply to the market you are interested in?
2. What does your intuition tell you about what phase the market might be in?
3. How might you test your intuition?
blocks.hint: Think about sales trends, number of competitors and how new the product is.
blocks.model: The answer depends on your market, but a good response names the phase (introduction, growth, maturity or decline), gives reasons such as the number and intensity of competitors, trend in sales, and how widely the offer is already adopted, and suggests tests such as market research, sales and industry data, trade press, talking to customers and watching competitors' behaviour.
points: Say which lifecycle phase you think the market is in and why
Use signs such as growth in sales, competitor numbers and profits
Test your intuition with market research, data and customer conversations
Acknowledge limits of a product-focused model; consider adoption groups too

blocks.text: Is the market for your offer already out there, or does your offer create an entirely new one? Unless your offer is something akin to the iPad, you will be competing in an existing market.

pages.title: How will you compete? Back to the Ps

blocks.text: Now draw together customers and markets and consider how to position your enterprise. This is highly contextual: for a social enterprise promoting a healthy diet, competition seems not quite the right concept, though you are competing for people's attention and against longstanding behaviours.

Getting the right mix of the seven Ps means engaging customers and matching the mix to different stages of development. Early on you might work with customers to get the product right, provide physical evidence of quality, get the people element right and find the optimum price.

blocks.title: Example: sandwiches
blocks.text: If your sandwich shop is surrounded by identical eateries, with no discernible difference in food, service or environment, your price may need to be competitive. An artisan baker selling sandwiches competes less on price than on fresh bread baked on the premises with traditional recipes and locally sourced fillings.

blocks.title: Activity 5 Differentiating your enterprise from the rest
blocks.prompt: Which Ps are dominant for your enterprise? Run through the seven Ps and think how you could positively differentiate your offer from others in relation to each of them. Then think where you want to be in the short term (a year), medium term (five years) and long term (ten years), and how your focus may switch.
blocks.hint: Product, price, place, promotion, people, process, physical evidence.
blocks.model: A strong answer works through each of the seven Ps, picks the one or two that matter most for the customers (for example product quality or convenience of place), says how you would stand out on each, and shows how the emphasis could change over time, e.g. from getting the product and price right in year one to brand, people and process as you grow.
points: Identify the dominant Ps for your enterprise
Describe a way to differentiate on each P
Set out short, medium and long term positions
Explain how your focus may shift as the enterprise matures

blocks.text: Earlier you looked at demographic factors, the shape of the market and how people compete. The maturity of the market, the size and number of competitors and the dimensions on which they compete all shape the market.
Some suggest adding products or services that are compatible with or complementary to yours. For example, there is a synergy between cars and the insurance industry that has an impact in each market.

blocks.title: Activity 6 What kind of organisation do you want to develop?
blocks.prompt:
What kind of organisation do you want to develop? Using the music analogy, what kind of band do you want to be?
- Playing to a small but loyal audience who love your music
- Loved by the critics with 'decent enough' sales
- Loyal to your fans and you would never sell them out
- Playing to 3000 plus, on TV, next stop Glastonbury
- Like The Stones: huge and still rolling on
- Beyonce
blocks.hint: There is no right answer: choose, and say what that means for how you compete.
blocks.model: There is no single right answer. A good response chooses one or more of the descriptions and links it to a strategy: a small loyal audience suggests a niche, close customer relationships and loyalty; mass-market stardom suggests scale, broad promotion and competing on a wide scale, and may mean not listening to early fans who liked the early stuff.
points: Choose the kind of organisation you want to be and why
Link the choice to your competitive position: niche or mass market
Consider who you would listen to as customers
Consider the trade-offs between loyalty and growth

blocks.text: Now it's time for the Session 4 badge quiz. It has fifteen questions, shown over the next five pages with three questions each. Answer them all.

blocks.title: Badge requirement
blocks.text: To earn the badge you need to score 50% or more in the Session 4 badge quiz (and in the Session 8 quiz). If you are not successful the first time, you can try again.

blocks.q: You buy a box of avocadoes for your 'pop up' café. In what sense are you a customer or consumer?
options: A customer but not a consumer
A consumer but not a customer
blocks.explain: You are purchasing the good, so you are the customer. You are not the one who uses it directly (your café's diners eat it), so you are not the consumer.

blocks.q: An employee uses stationery that is bought centrally by the organisation. The employee is:
options: The customer but not the consumer
A consumer but not the buying customer
blocks.explain: Consumers use a product; customers purchase it. The employee uses the stationery but did not buy it.

blocks.q: Why is the term 'client' increasingly used in the public and third sector?
options: Because it suggests a mutual expectation and a stake each side has in the relationship
Because it is a legal requirement
Because it implies a one-off transaction
blocks.explain: 'Client' signals mutual expectations and recognises the stake each party has in the relationship.

blocks.q: Which of these is the main aim of a focus group?
options: To gather qualitative feedback from small groups through facilitated discussion
To sell the product to the participants
blocks.explain: Focus groups are facilitated group discussions that gather qualitative feedback and a deeper understanding of issues, if well moderated.

blocks.q: Because an entrepreneur is close to their own customer experience, they can safely assume they are typical of their target customers.
blocks.explain: It is right to urge caution: you can only know whether you are representative by engaging with potential customers.

blocks.q: Which statements about 'personas' are correct? Select all that apply.
options: They are detailed descriptions of perfect or even difficult customers
They are often based on real information
They are used to inform decisions on how different groups might be treated
They are legal contracts with customers
blocks.explain: Personas are detailed, often evidence-based descriptions of customers that feed into the development process. They are not contracts.

blocks.q: In the Reinartz and Kumar Loyalty Model, which segment has high profit potential but is short-term, so you should milk the account only while it is active?
blocks.explain: Butterflies are a good fit with high profit potential but short-term; aim for transactional satisfaction and cease investing soon enough.

blocks.q: Which segment is long-term but low profit, where you should measure the size and share of wallet?
blocks.explain: Barnacles are limited fit, low profit, long-term customers. Measure size and share of wallet, then up- or cross-sell, or control costs strictly.

blocks.q: Which of the customer-oriented four Cs corresponds to 'Place'?
blocks.explain: Place corresponds to Convenience; Price to Cost, Promotion to Communication and Product to Customer needs/wants.

blocks.q: Which of these is NOT one of the original seven Ps of the marketing mix as shown in the session?
blocks.explain: The seven Ps are product, price, place, promotion, people, process and physical evidence. Profit is not one of them.

blocks.q: Which characteristic is a 'decision-making process' consideration when describing a market?
options: The size of other businesses in it
Who makes the purchase decision and what or who influences them
blocks.explain: Decision-making process asks who makes the purchase decision, what influences them and what we know about them. The others are geography, demographics and behaviour.

blocks.q: In the market lifecycle, which phase is characterised by small sales and difficulty making a profit because of the cost of taking the offer to market?
blocks.explain: In introduction, sales are small and profit is hard because of the costs of taking the offer to market.

blocks.q: In the maturity phase of the market lifecycle:
options: Sales are rapidly growing and new competitors are arriving
Sales growth tails away and plateaus, profits are still present but competition may be intense
blocks.explain: Maturity sees growth tail away then plateau, with profits still present but intense competition.

blocks.q: Rogers' technology adoption curve focuses on:
options: The consumer, showing when successive customer groups enter the market
The legal structure of the business
blocks.explain: Rogers focuses on the consumer rather than the product, and on how to move consumers from awareness through persuasion, trialling and adoption to consolidation.

blocks.q: When your artisan bakery sells sandwiches using fresh bread baked on the premises, price may be a less dominant factor than for a sandwich shop whose offer is identical to its neighbours'.
blocks.explain: Where you offer differentiated value, you need not compete mainly on price; if your offer is the same as others, price may need to be competitive.

blocks.text: In this session you have:

items: identified the customers that your business is aimed at
described in detail the market you are competing in and its characteristics
defined who you think you will be competing with.

blocks.text: You may feel you are already close to your customer, but there is more listening to be done. Return to your idea and refine it in relation to customer needs and the competitive forces in the market.

blocks.title: Is the customer always right?
blocks.text: Not always. When a new product creates a new market, your intuition may be a better judge than people less invested in change. Be careful which customers you listen to: if you want to be the biggest band in the world, it might not pay to listen to the loyal fans who liked your early stuff.

Even so, the customer, client or consumer belongs at the centre as the most important stakeholder in your business model. Being close to them, to changes in taste, technology and markets, and to unmet needs is a key advantage of being small. Use these insights to develop the customer relationships, customer segments and value proposition parts of your canvas. The value proposition comes up next in Session 5.

chapters.title: Defining and building the value proposition
chapters.summary: Learn what a value proposition is, how mutual value is created across four dimensions, and how to write your own boilerplate value proposition.

blocks.text: Why do some businesses succeed when others don't? Where do they draw their advantage from? The answers lie in the concept of the **value proposition**. In this session you will consider where value is derived in a business, how to build it into a proposition for customers and how to ensure it is sustainable for your business.

Value is an interesting concept - like beauty, it is in the eye of the beholder. Where you think your idea adds value may differ from where potential customers look for it. In the end, value is measured by how much people are willing to pay for something.

blocks.title: By the end of this session you will be able to
blocks.text: Explain what a value proposition is; define and build one for your own enterprise; and demonstrate how it can differentiate your business from others for a competitive edge.

In Session 3 the business model canvas placed the value proposition at the centre of your business model. It answers the question: what is it you are trying to build, and for whom? It goes beyond an idea or product and expands to:

items: what problem(s) or need(s) you are solving or meeting for customers
how your idea will either alleviate the problem or provide a gain for customers
who the customers are whose needs or problems you are focused on.

blocks.text: The best value propositions are clear about these points and provide a compelling reason for a big enough group of customers to choose your business, product or service over another.

The **spreadsheet** was originally developed for accountants to organise and manipulate a lot of complex data that would otherwise be very time-consuming and problematic to do manually. It solves the problems of complexity, manual data inputting, errors and duplication of data. A convenient technological resolution to a problem, it has now been adopted by a much wider audience.

As human beings we have many different kinds of need, such as the need to be entertained, to socialise and communicate with others. **Social media apps** arguably provide a solution to some of these needs.
Where you solve a universal need, the target audience could be very large indeed, as opposed to a very niche group of customers.

Arguably, the recent pandemic and lockdown, and the prevailing economic conditions, have taught us that our perceptions of value can change. The concept of the frontline or essential worker has shifted attitudes to work, and the furlough scheme has changed dynamics in many ways.

Shortages and delivery difficulties in supply chains create headaches for businesses and customers, but also opportunities along the chain. The shift to working from home, alternative ways of delivering services and the rise in online shopping mean major shifts in customer attitudes and behaviour - and a need for businesses to reflect on their business models and value propositions.

pages.title: Activity 1: A major event and your idea

blocks.title: Activity 1 Reflecting on how a major event impacts on your idea
blocks.prompt: Take a few minutes (about 10) to consider how a major event such as the Covid-19 pandemic has had an impact on your life as a consumer or customer. Have you noticed a shift in your own values, buying behaviour or priorities? How do they impact on your choice of suppliers and your own notions of value?
blocks.hint: Think about what you buy, who you buy it from, and what has become more or less important to you.
blocks.model: Even in a crisis, opportunities arise for some people and businesses. Lockdown brought a rise in pet ownership (3.2 million UK households added a pet, with shortages of dog and cat food), restaurants and pubs pivoted to takeaway, grocery delivery slots were scarce, and millions equipped themselves to work from home, boosting home office furnishings and internet needs. Reported: 51% of furloughed UK employees were considering a career change, and some will have decided to pursue their own business idea.
points: A major event can shift your own values, buying behaviour and priorities
Changing priorities change which suppliers you choose and what you see as valuable
Shortages and new needs (e.g. home working, delivery, pets) create opportunities for businesses
Businesses should revisit their value proposition when customer attitudes shift

blocks.text: Not all customers are the same. Some have greater need, use or preference for your products or services. Some bring greater financial gain, some make more demands on your customer service and some are more profitable. Even before you start trading, it helps to consider the types of customer you may attract.

A second consideration is what support customers need to buy from you initially and afterwards. If your product is a one-off or infrequent purchase, value may come from other sources: follow-up supplies, refills, upgrades.
Coffee machine and printer manufacturers have changed their business models: the hardware has become relatively cheap and the revenue comes from repeat purchases of coffee pods and cartridges.

blocks.alt: Image of coffee pods.
blocks.caption: Figure 1 Repeat purchases, such as coffee pods, have helped businesses increase revenue.

blocks.text: A third consideration is how far your product or idea is 'unique' or different from others in the marketplace. Not all successful businesses are unique in all regards - they find competitive advantage from another source.
Your business may not uniquely solve a problem customers have, but it may reduce the **friction** they currently experience in dealing with other suppliers.

blocks.title: Example
blocks.text: Technology and mobile phone companies have entered financial services. Phone apps have made banking, saving and payments much easier than ten years ago. The basic service (e.g. making a payment) is the same, but the user experience is very different.
As you think about your business idea, you might increase value for customers across four dimensions: **strategic**, **economic**, **operational** and **behavioural**.

blocks.alt: Diagram with Mutual Value at the centre, linked to four circles: Strategic, Economic, Behavioural and Operational.
blocks.caption: Figure 2 Dimensions of value (adapted from Parvatiyar and Seth, 2001)

blocks.title: Strategic value
blocks.text: The more aligned you are with your customers' needs and wants, and the more relevant a place you have in their lives, the more likely you are to succeed. Your values, brand, ways of working and the product itself are a good fit with your target audiences.

blocks.title: Economic value
blocks.text: For your business: achieving a price that exceeds the cost of providing the product or service, which requires efficiency in sourcing, providing and serving. For the customer: paying a price they think is worth paying relative to alternative solutions to their need or problem.

Customers come into contact with your business in a variety of ways, sometimes called **customer touchpoints**. Wherever and whenever they touch your business there is an opportunity to reinforce the value of what is offered (and, with poor service, to detract from it).
In today's world, where people are considered time poor, this means making it convenient and easy for customers to deal with you.

blocks.title: Reflection: easy to deal with?
blocks.prompt: Take about 5 minutes to reflect on how many suppliers or providers you deal with as a customer. How do they perform on this dimension of being easy to deal with? What is it they do - or don't do - that makes dealing with them good or bad?
blocks.model: You may have thought of opening hours, convenient location, or self-service so you can deal with suppliers at the time that suits you. You may also have thought about efficient processes - for example being 'remembered' as a returning customer so you don't repeat your details or request - or recognition and rewards for loyalty where the company uses your data to good effect.
points: Convenience such as opening hours, location or self-service
Efficient processes, e.g. being remembered as a returning customer
Recognition or loyalty rewards that use customer data well
Poor or missing touchpoints make a supplier harder to deal with

blocks.text: There are many ways to set up your organisation to give a smoother, more effective experience that adds value and differentiates you from others.

The whole banking industry has been turned upside down by mobile banking, attracting many new businesses that are not banks, such as Apple (Apple Pay), Amazon and Alibaba. You can move money, pay, receive money, exchange currencies and even use cryptocurrencies at the touch of your smartphone.

For many people, apps and cashless payments are more secure, efficient, convenient and cheaper than visiting a distant branch to deposit or withdraw cash, pay in cheques or exchange money. Even so, for some transactions the human touch is preferable to technology.
You can probably remember occasions when a member of staff left a good or bad impression, and how it made you feel - from satisfaction or delight to frustration and annoyance.

For most businesses there is a real benefit in encouraging customer satisfaction and even delight. Happy customers come back, and delighted customers will tell other people. The flip side: unhappy customers tend to be more vociferous in telling people about bad experiences.
To retain customers and grow your business, it pays to be attentive to customer expectations and the customer experience.

Value is more than cost and price, and comes from more than your product or service. It is the sum total of what you provide for customers, delivered through all the elements of your business model. Your business should create value people want or need at the right price, so there is an exchange of value - customers pay you for all that you give them.
For a viable value proposition, refer back to Session 4 to understand:

items: who and where your target audience is
how they perceive the offer, and how you can shape that perception
how the offer can be positioned relative to competing products, services or suppliers, in terms of features and benefits
how to communicate this value meaningfully, emphasising what they care about most.

pages.title: Do you know enough about your audience?

blocks.text: Before describing your value proposition, pause: how would you describe your target audience? How much do you know about their needs or problems, and the difference your idea would make to them? Would it persuade them to change their buying or usage behaviour? Does it save enough time, or provide enough benefit, to change habits or suppliers, or to pay more?
If you don't know, you may need more research among potential customers (recall the focus group activity in Session 4), or to understand where competition will come from and its value proposition.

blocks.title: Competition can be unexpected
blocks.text: A competing product may be unrelated to how you classify your own. A car that runs on alternative fuels competes with petrol or diesel cars, but for some customers also with bicycles, public transport and taxis.

blocks.alt: A pack of six red soft rollerball pens, 'Nib', fine nib 1.0 mm, RRP 1.95, with recycling and CE marks.
blocks.caption: Figure 3 More than a pen?

blocks.title: Activity 2 Feature or benefit? (part 1)
blocks.prompt: List at least four features of the product shown above - properties or aspects of its design. Then for each feature provide a customer benefit. (Hint: complete the sentence 'which means that...'.)
blocks.hint: Look at the price, nib, ink colour, packaging and symbols on the pack.
blocks.model: The pen is affordably priced, which means you don't have to worry about losing it as it can be replaced cheaply; it has a fine nib, so it can be used for handwriting or fine detailed work; it uses red ink, which means writing or marking stands out more than black or blue; it is packaged in recycled packaging, so it creates less damage to the environment; the quality standard ensures a minimum standard accepted throughout the European market, which gives assurance of the materials used.
points: Affordable price, so cheap to replace if lost
Fine nib, so suits handwriting and detailed work
Red ink, so writing stands out
Recycled packaging, so less environmental damage
Quality standard (CE mark), so assurance of materials

blocks.title: Activity 2 Feature or benefit? (part 2)
blocks.prompt: If this was your product, how might you express the value to customers of this product in no more than 100 words? (Look back at Session 3 for tips.)
blocks.hint: Lead with the benefit to the customer, not the feature.
blocks.model: A short, benefit-led statement works best. The source suggests something like: 'A cost-effective pen that doesn't cost the planet.' Think of your own product in this way and make notes about your value proposition. The purpose is to think as your customers do: what is important to them, and how you could persuade them that you provide enough value to pay your price, switch behaviour or supplier, or try something new.
points: Express the value from the customer's point of view
Combine key benefits (e.g. low cost and environmental friendliness)
Keep it short, clear and memorable
Make it persuasive enough to justify paying or switching

blocks.text: How customers make their choice is vital to understand if you are to communicate the value of your business. Sometimes features or benefits are so unique they are memorable and lead to a point of difference people will pay more for. They may even be patented.

items: The mint with the hole: unique, memorable and a trademark.
A coffee jar of a particular shape with a reusable seal: unique features that add value and encourage loyalty beyond the taste of the coffee.

blocks.title: USP
blocks.text: A unique selling proposition: a feature or benefit unique enough to be memorable and to give a point of difference.

Think of trainers: was the decision really based only on price? Where there are multiple products in the same price range, the label or brand is often as important. A brand may confer a certain value or imply the wearer's values and style - classic, high quality, trendy and popular. Customers tend to pay more for this association.
Some household names have become 'genericised' - Hoover became a verb, as has Google.

A good brand name sticks in the minds of prospective customers, but this takes a lot of time, marketing and communications activity, and often budget. It can be very hard for a new business to establish a brand from a standing start.

blocks.title: Reflection: brand and USP
blocks.prompt: Before defining a value proposition for your own idea (or one for a product or service you know), consider: In what ways can a product or company name suggest something about what customers will experience? Can it convey a particular image or suggest something that separates it from others? How do brands and USPs impact on price and on the customer's perception of value?
blocks.model: A name can hint at the experience, quality or values of a product and create an image that separates it from rivals. Strong brands and USPs let customers associate the product with certain values, so they are often prepared to pay more and perceive greater value. Building a brand, however, takes time and money.
points: A name can signal qualities, image and values
It can differentiate the product from others in the market
Strong brands and USPs support higher prices
They raise the customer's perception of value

blocks.text: Listen to how our entrepreneurs have thought through their value proposition and how useful it is as a concept. Take notes in a notebook as ideas occur. What did they say?

blocks.title: Video 1 Value proposition
blocks.note: Entrepreneurs (Emma Prince, Claudio Marturano, Nick Allen, Alex Bond) describe their value propositions: meeting a local need and evolving it as the company grows; bite-sized on-shift regulatory training that saves organisations tens of thousands of pounds; high-quality, detailed designs that bring happiness; and cutting a quarter of hygiene-auditing costs. They say a clear value proposition is a conversation starter, gives clarity to customers and helps you steer away from what you're not useful for.

blocks.text: Describe a business or product idea you have been thinking of. It doesn't have to be real. Here is a fictitious example.

To parents of young active toddlers, our new 'Peekapoo' disposable nappies contain a microchip and are made of completely disposable materials that allow you to not only save the planet but also keep track of where your precious little one is hiding using our unique tracking technology on your phone.

items: Target customer group: 'parents of young, active children'.
Brand name: 'Peekapoo'.
New concept: the microchip in the environmentally friendly nappy.
Distinct from other renewable nappies: green credentials plus tracking your baby on your phone.

blocks.title: Activity 3 Creating a 'boilerplate' description
blocks.prompt: With reference to the example, create a 'boilerplate' description for your business or product idea (or a fictitious one) by completing: To [target group and the need you serve] our [product, service or brand] is [the concept or product/service category] that [your organisation's or product's unique or distinctive feature].
blocks.hint: Allow about 10 minutes. Fill each blank in turn.
blocks.model: Example following the template: 'To parents of young active toddlers, our Peekapoo nappies are an environmentally friendly disposable nappy with a built-in microchip that lets you track your child on your phone.' A good answer names the target group and need, the brand and category, and one distinctive feature.
points: Names the target group and the need served
States the product, service or brand and its category
Gives a unique or distinctive feature
Is clear and concise enough to test on others

blocks.text: Defining, describing and communicating your value proposition may take more time than you think. Try testing a few versions on friends, family or trusted advisers until you think you have got it right.

blocks.title: Try it: build your value proposition
blocks.intro: Map the customer's jobs, pains and gains against what you offer, and see whether your value proposition really fits what they care about.

blocks.text: Products and businesses are the basis of a **mutual value exchange** with customers. You must persuade customers that what you have is valuable enough to pay your price, or to change their behaviour: trialling a product, changing supplier or doing something in a completely different way.

items: learned the key concept of the value proposition
attempted to define a value proposition for your own idea, which you will refine
considered how it may differentiate you from competitors, provided customers understand the value for them.

blocks.text: Some ways of adding value cost nothing (a positive, customer-friendly attitude); others, like special packaging or an exclusive outlet, add cost. Balance the value you provide against the price and volume you can expect so that value stays mutual.

blocks.q: Which best describes a value proposition?
options: A list of your products and their prices
The answer to what you are building and for whom, covering the problem or need solved and the gain provided
A forecast of your first-year profit
blocks.explain: A value proposition goes beyond an idea or product: it covers the problem or need, how your idea alleviates it or provides a gain, and who the customers are.

blocks.q: Coffee machine and printer makers earn much of their revenue from pods and cartridges. This illustrates:
options: Value created from repeat purchases and follow-up supplies
A one-off premium price for hardware
blocks.explain: Where the product is a one-off purchase, value can come from other sources such as refills, consumables and upgrades.

blocks.q: Which are the four dimensions of mutual value shown in Figure 2?
blocks.explain: The dimensions of value are strategic, economic, operational and behavioural (adapted from Parvatiyar and Seth, 2001). The other options are the marketing mix, STEEPLE letters and VIRO.

blocks.q: Making it convenient and easy for customers at every touchpoint is an example of which dimension of value?
blocks.explain: Operational value is about customer touchpoints and being easy to deal with, especially for time-poor customers.

blocks.q: A benefit describes a property of the design of a product, while a feature describes what it means for the customer.
blocks.explain: It is the other way round: a feature is a property or aspect of the design; the benefit is what it means for the customer ('which means that...').

blocks.q: A new business can easily build a strong brand from a standing start.
blocks.explain: A good brand takes a lot of time, marketing and communications activity, and often budget, so it is hard for a new business to establish.

chapters.title: Aligning resources to opportunities
chapters.summary: Scan the external environment, understand your transformation processes, and align resources and capabilities to build and sustain a competitive advantage.

blocks.text: How do you ensure that you are playing to your strengths? How can you be sure you are maximising your chances of success? The answers often come down to how well you analyse opportunities, how objective you are about your context and, of course, good judgement and good luck.

Having examined your value proposition, you now consider how to align the resources you have and develop the capabilities of your enterprise. The session looks at the fit between the external environment and the internal environment - that which you are creating - with the internal environment as the main focus.

blocks.title: By the end of this session you will be able to
blocks.text: Apply an environmental analysis to spot opportunities or threats; recognise the kinds of transformation process in your enterprise; recognise the resources and capabilities you have or might develop; and appreciate their alignment and potential as a source of innovation and sustained competitive advantage.

blocks.alt: A burning meteor travelling towards Earth.
blocks.caption: Figure 1 Are there challenges heading your way?

blocks.text: When starting an enterprise, first scan the external environment for forthcoming threats or opportunities that could affect the timing of your launch or whether to enter a market. Consider the nature of competition and whether one market is more attractive than others.
One well-known acronym for environmental scans is **STEEPLE**: Social, Technical, Economic, Environmental, Political, Legal, Ethical.

blocks.alt: Building blocks spelling STEEPLE: Social, Technical, Economic, Environmental, Political, Legal, Ethical.
blocks.caption: Figure 2 STEEPLE

blocks.text: Consider the factors that are most dominant for your circumstances - those with the greatest potential to provide opportunities or threats.

items: **Social:** an ageing society or a low birth rate. Thinking back to Session 3, what implications would this have for SAGA, who target the older population, in the short and longer term? And for a baby food manufacturer?
**Political:** policy changes, nationalisation, large infrastructure projects.
**Legal:** regulation.
**Economic:** trends in employment, or a change in taxation.
Environmental, technological and ethical factors are more self-explanatory.

blocks.text: The main thing is to understand the rate of change and the extent of impact on your sector and market.
'Porter's Five Forces' (Porter, 2008) is often used to assess the rivalry in a given market as a clue to how you need to position yourself.

blocks.alt: Competition (rivalry amongst firms) at the centre, surrounded by threat of new entrants, bargaining power of suppliers, bargaining power of buyers, threat from substitutes, and complements.
blocks.caption: Figure 3 Porter's Five Forces and complements (adapted from Porter, 2008)

blocks.text: As a new entrant you might use the forces to assess an existing market. For a coffee shop, the cost of entry might be low (depending on location), but you would think carefully about suppliers, particularly discounts and credit.

You would probably be most concerned about **substitutes** and **buyer power**: coffee chains are well established and others have branched into lifestyle - working space or healthy alternatives such as chai-based drinks and juice bars.

blocks.title: Complements
blocks.text: Coffee and books seem a staple on the high street now; more than one independent has evolved into a cafe, internet cafe or bookshop with cafe over the last 20 years.

pages.title: Activity 1: How useful is the theory?

blocks.text: Enterprises need to reflect the outside world and how it is changing. If you have not used STEEPLE, Porter's Five Forces or similar scanning tools, try them now.

blocks.title: Activity 1 How useful is the theory in practice? (part 1)
blocks.prompt: Thinking of your own business idea or enterprise, make some notes using either or both of the scanning tools (STEEPLE, Porter's Five Forces) or another one you know. Allow about 20 minutes.
blocks.hint: Pick the two or three STEEPLE factors or forces with the greatest potential impact on your sector.
blocks.model: A good answer picks the most dominant factors for your circumstances, for example social (ageing population), economic (taxation changes) or legal (regulation), and for Five Forces identifies the most threatening forces, such as substitutes, buyer power or new entrants, plus any complements.
points: Identifies the most dominant external factors for the sector
Distinguishes opportunities from threats
Considers rate of change and impact on the market
Considers competition, substitutes and complements

blocks.title: Activity 1 How useful is the theory in practice? (part 2)
blocks.prompt: Having tried to use either STEEPLE or Porter's Five Forces, how useful did you find them?
blocks.model: Focusing on the rapidly changing external environment alone can leave you wondering how to respond - nobody tells you what to do. One criticism is that if you worry about what others are doing, who is worrying about what you are doing? Another is that the analysis is a snapshot in time: how often will you repeat it? And who decides which issues matter most? You do. Despite this, if you never consider external factors, like the meteor in Figure 1 you may not see the trouble heading your way.
points: The tools do not tell you what to do - you must decide the response
They are only a snapshot in time, so must be repeated
You decide which issues are more or less important
Ignoring external factors altogether risks missing threats

blocks.text: Being concerned about how you create value and the unique way you compete leads to greater diversity, because every individual or group has a different set of resources and capabilities. This session focuses on that approach.
Before looking at it in detail, you need a clearer view of what happens inside an enterprise: what kinds of **transformation process** occur.

In Session 3 business was introduced as a value delivery system with inputs and outputs. As enterprises attend ever more closely to customers, don't forget the bit between the big idea and someone using it - transformation, production or operations.

blocks.alt: Inputs arrow, transformation process box, outputs arrow, with a feedback loop from outputs back to inputs.
blocks.caption: Figure 4 Transformation of inputs to outputs

blocks.text: In this simplified model, inputs fall into three main types:

items: **materials** - physical things you turn from one state into another
**information** - part of the process or transformed through it
**people** - who through engagement are transformed in some way.

blocks.text: Transformation is not just turning raw material into something else: an accountant turns receipts and invoices into financial statements; a personal trainer makes you fitter. The middle stage involves configuring **facilities** (land, premises, machines, equipment) and **people** (staff or contractors directly involved). Organising inputs and aligning resources into capabilities gives an output.
When something physical is made, it is easy to see what is transformed. For services based on people or information it is less clear. Transformation processes can include:

head: Change in...
Example
rows: physical characteristics of materials or customers
location of materials, information or customers
physiological or psychological state of customers

blocks.text: Organisations often transform a series of inputs. In a class on making a chair, it is not simply the wood that is transformed - tacit information about making a chair becomes explicit and you acquire skills and perhaps a feeling of well-being. Transformation can be categorised as:

items: **manufacture** - the physical creation of products
**transportation** - movement of materials or customers
**supply** - change of ownership
**service** - the way customers are treated, or storage of materials.

blocks.text: The overall transformation typically involves a series of smaller transformations with different inputs. The social enterprise **Social Bite** operates sandwich shops and deliveries to address homelessness. It involves:

items: the transformation of raw materials through food preparation
customer service that goes beyond basic needs, as customers know their purchases help the homeless
the supply of sandwiches to different locations
supporting the transformation of its employees through employment and training of the homeless.

blocks.title: Activity 2 What transformation is involved?
blocks.prompt: Select a business idea from our entrepreneurs or use your own enterprise. Sketch out the kinds of transformation processes involved, using three columns: Input, Transformation process, Output (aim for several rows). Allow about 5 minutes.
blocks.hint: Remember inputs can be materials, information or people.
blocks.model: Look back at how you described the processes and reflect on the business model and value proposition. Can you identify where in the transformation process the value is built, and who makes that happen? Perhaps you can see ways to add value for customers, make things more efficient and reduce costs - which may point to where you can innovate.
points: Lists inputs (materials, information, people) and outputs
Describes what transforms them (change of form, location, ownership, state)
Identifies where value is built and by whom
Spots ways to add value or reduce cost, pointing to innovation

blocks.text: So far there has been deliberate language about resources and developing capabilities by aligning them. These are specific to you or your organisation, which makes them hard for others to imitate - perhaps because they are tacit, or because only you have access to them, such as a component, recipe or location. Resources can be:

items: **tangible** - physical, like a workshop or a machine
**intangible** - 'know how', your reputation, work culture
**human** - the people you work with and their skills.

blocks.text: Critical questions: how you use the resources you have, how you acquire those you need, and how you configure them to make your enterprise different - creating strategic value (Session 5).

pages.title: Revisit your canvas: key resources and partners

blocks.title: Try it: key resources and key partners
blocks.intro: Return to your business model canvas and review the Key Resources and Key Partners boxes. Tag each resource as tangible, intangible or human, and note what you might get partners to do instead.

blocks.text: Enterprises need the right people, and that assessment of the right person for the right job includes the entrepreneur. In your own enterprise the separation between intangible and human resources may seem artificial, as it may only be you and what you know.

Perhaps you can do it all: think of ideas, make them happen, attract funding, keep things running and advocate for the company. But as an enterprise grows you will need to work with others. One way to find the right people is to think about the **jobs that need to be done**.

pages.title: Job needs analysis (1): role and purpose

blocks.text: In Activity 3 you will think in terms of a job, or series of jobs. You won't consider the attributes of an entrepreneur here (see Further reading for links). Imagine advertising your own job using the job needs analysis below. Start with:
Job role

items: What tasks are required to produce the product or service?
What tasks are required to sell it?
What tasks are required to support production and sales staff?
Which of these tasks need to be done in-house?

blocks.text: Purpose of job

items: How does it contribute to successful production of the product?
How does it contribute to successful sale of the product?
How does it contribute to achieving the aims of the firm?

blocks.text: Essential functions

items: What key tasks actually form the job? Are they all essential?
How are the key tasks related to each other? Is there a sequence?
What physical activities need to be performed?
Can the activities be shared among a number of people?
How much time is spent on each task?
Are the tasks equally important to completing the job?
What happens if a task is not completed?

pages.title: Job needs analysis (3): qualifications and context

blocks.text: Job qualifications

items: Are formal qualifications required?
Is specialist knowledge required?
What are the skills required?
What training is required?
What previous experience is required?

blocks.text: Job context

items: Where are the essential tasks done?
How is the work organised?
What are the physical and social conditions?
How is the job supervised?

blocks.text: *(Source: The Open University, 2018)*

blocks.title: Activity 3 Job analysis
blocks.prompt: Imagine you had to advertise your own job, based on the job needs analysis. What would you put in the essential criteria and what in the desirable ones? What specific capabilities are needed, and how do these create value for customers? Allow about 15 minutes.
blocks.hint: Work through role, purpose, essential functions, qualifications and context.
blocks.model: The source gives no model answer. A good response separates must-have criteria (the key tasks, skills and knowledge without which the job cannot be done) from desirable ones (nice-to-have experience or qualifications), and links each capability to the value it creates for customers, such as quality, speed, or service.
points: Separates essential from desirable criteria
Draws on tasks for production, sales and support
Names specific skills, knowledge or experience required
Links capabilities to value created for customers

blocks.text: If this was useful, apply the same process to another role. If family or friends do a job, it could help start a conversation about how well they perform it.

As your business develops you may need to look outside for specialist skills or experience. Anticipate tensions in a team due to disagreements about expectations, performance and capabilities. If you resolve to discuss them openly and honestly, you can become a stronger team.

Using the job needs analysis questions and discussing them together is a more objective way of talking things through. Allied to this is **culture**: perhaps the fit between person and role matters less than how well they fit the culture you create, deliberately or by example.

Recognising how the resources you have (or can readily access) relate to an opportunity, and deploying them effectively, is an important part of success. Physical resources may seem easier to acquire and align than human ones - but they have their own challenges.

blocks.alt: A man in a workshop carving wood to make a chair.
blocks.caption: Figure 5 Resources are interrelated

blocks.text: Resources are interrelated. Think of the chair-making class: human resources, machines, location, reputation, quality of materials and 'know how' all link together. The link between 'know how' and tangible resources can be difficult to untangle.

In a knowledge economy it is easy to forget that realigning tangible resources can be a source of innovation and competitive advantage. Tech companies can disrupt whole markets using technology to meet unmet demand, often at a lower price point or by dispensing with superfluous service (Christensen et al., 2015).

blocks.title: Disruptive innovation
blocks.text: A smaller company with fewer resources successfully challenges an established large player by offering alternatives, often at lower cost and with broader customer appeal. This often draws new customers into the market. Think of reducing 'friction' and increasing convenience, as in the mobile banking example in Session 5.
Gans (2016) differentiates two forms of disruption.

items: **Demand-led:** new features or functionality go on to change what customers look for in a product (e.g. cheaper or more efficient).

**Supply-side:** a radically different approach or new technology changes how things are done. Example: Apple entering the smartphone market, letting people go beyond text messaging and email, which BlackBerry had done well until then. Apple effectively provided a handheld computer.

blocks.text: Over time products and services develop set ways of doing things and improve incrementally. Your specialist capabilities or access to particular resources may be a source of competitive advantage.

A lot is written about how incumbents can compete with new entrants engaged in disruptive innovation, but the idea applies to new enterprises too. Entrepreneurs often have a new way of looking at things, and in Sessions 1 and 4 it was suggested that being close to your customers is a key advantage - you might be 'a customer' who sees a way to improve things.

Another source of innovation is new ways of delivering value, putting products or services together differently and disrupting existing routines. How disruptive will you be? Will you change the way others operate? What in your business model might they seek to imitate?

Tangible resources are easier to name; intangible ones are harder. Sometimes tangible and intangible resources complement each other and produce more than the sum of their parts; sometimes they combine badly (any long-suffering sports fan will recognise this).
Grant (2010) suggests that to put resources together successfully you think through four things, explained here using a restaurant.

head: Element
Restaurant example
rows: Processes: the sequence of actions that enable transformation
Deciding a recipe and quantities, sourcing food, preparing, cooking, presenting, serving, taking payment
Organisational structure: how well it is co-ordinated
Is food prep in the restaurant kitchen? Is buying central? Does one kitchen prepare for several restaurants?
Motivation: whether people can be effective
Are waiting staff trained, do they know the menu and recommend drinks, is there a reward system such as tips?
Alignment: fit with customer wants and needs
Good location with high footfall, ability to recruit staff, local and sustainable sourcing meeting demand and quality

blocks.text: Mapping is not simple and may take time, but is worth doing. Examining a corporate giant like Walmart, which looks like a grocer that went global, you find one reason it out-competed others on price and stock was being very good at logistics - the right product in the right place at the right time.

blocks.title: Activity 4 Mapping resources and capability
blocks.prompt: Map out your resources and think through the capabilities of your organisation (or one you know). (1) Organisational capabilities overall; (2) Process, Organisational structure, Motivation, Organisational alignment; (3) Resources: Tangible, Intangible, Human. Allow about 40 minutes.
blocks.hint: There is no feedback in the source for this activity - use the restaurant example as a guide.
blocks.model: The source gives no model answer. A good map names tangible (premises, equipment), intangible (know how, reputation, culture) and human resources, then describes how processes, structure, motivation and alignment combine them into capabilities that fit customers' needs, as Walmart's logistics did.
points: Lists tangible, intangible and human resources
Describes processes and organisational structure
Considers motivation of people
Shows alignment of resources with customer needs
Names the overall capability that makes the organisation different

blocks.text: How will you sustain any competitive advantage you create? You have mainly looked internally so far, at the resources you have and need, aligning them and what makes them distinctive. To sustain advantage, first keep an eye on both internal and external environments, as advantage can erode over time.

blocks.title: VIRO
blocks.text: Are the capabilities and resources you can access: Valuable (to the enterprise)? Inimitable (difficult to imitate)? Rare (hard to acquire)? Organisational (organised so you can take advantage of and exploit them)?

blocks.title: Activity 5 Maintaining competitive advantage
blocks.prompt: Pick one resource or capability you believe is a point of differentiation for your enterprise (or one you know). Put it into the framework, answering Y or N for: Valuable, Rare, Inimitable, Exploited by the organisation. Then say what the implication is. Allow about 20 minutes.
blocks.model: The standard answers: N on Valuable means disadvantage; Y then N on Rare means parity; Y, Y, N on Inimitable means temporary advantage; Y, Y, Y, N on Exploited means advantage insufficiently used; Y on all four means sustained advantage. It is the process - the discussions that lead to filling in the blanks - that helps most.
points: Answers Y or N for valuable, rare, inimitable and exploited
Reads the implication correctly (disadvantage, parity, temporary, insufficiently used or sustained advantage)
Gives reasons for each answer
Notes what to do if the resource is not fully exploited

blocks.text: Like any of these tools, it is the discussion that leads to filling in the blanks that helps most.

The skill in developing an enterprise is ensuring resources and capabilities match the **key success factors** in a given area. Grant (2010) suggests addressing them by asking about customers and competition.

items: Customers: Who are they? What do they want?
Competition: Who are the competition? What are the main dimensions of competition? What drives it and what is the intensity?

blocks.text: These questions ask how you position yourself against customers and competitors to ensure survival - how your internal organisation is aligned with the external environment, which should be considered together. You must also learn to find your own sources of information about the external environment.

blocks.title: Activity 6 Your key success factors
blocks.prompt: Map out your key success factors. Build on your ideas about what customers want as part of an analysis of demand, assess how organisations survive and prosper in your part of the market through external scans of market and competition, then map the factors onto your resources and capabilities. Allow about 15 minutes.
blocks.hint: If you are creating a completely new market, consider current alternatives, or a vacuum of competition.
blocks.model: The source gives no model answer. Note that some enterprises find this easier than others. If you are creating a new market, it may be harder to discern competition; think about what alternatives exist now and consider that there may be an absence of competition, or that your venture may not be looking to compete.
points: States who customers are and what they want
Identifies competitors and the dimensions of competition
Lists the key success factors in your market
Maps each factor onto specific resources and capabilities
Notes gaps where resources or capabilities must be acquired

blocks.text: This session focused on the alignment of resources and capabilities. The way you align them is what makes you different - perhaps 'the difference that makes a difference'.

items: considered the external environment and how it impacts your enterprise over time
recognised your internal capabilities and resources and how to align them for competitive advantage
recognised that sustaining advantage means staying aware of both internal and external environments
identified your key success factors.

blocks.text: Think through your partners, what you are good at and what you might get others to do, and reflect on the key resources and capabilities you have and those you need to acquire. One key resource is finance - the next session explores it.

blocks.q: What do the letters in the acronym STEEPLE stand for?
options: Social, Technical, Economic, Environmental, Political, Legal, Ethical
Strategy, Trade, Equity, Entry, Price, Logistics, Exports
Sales, Targets, Earnings, Expenses, Profit, Loans, Equity
Suppliers, Timing, Exchange, Economy, Pricing, Laws, Ethics
blocks.explain: STEEPLE is an environmental scanning tool covering the Social, Technical, Economic, Environmental, Political, Legal and Ethical factors.

blocks.q: Which are forces in Porter's Five Forces model as shown in Figure 3? Select all that apply.
blocks.explain: The forces include rivalry, new entrants, supplier and buyer power and substitutes (with complements). Motivation is part of Grant's resource alignment, not Porter's forces.

blocks.q: An accountant turning receipts and invoices into financial statements is an example of transformation.
blocks.explain: Transformation is not just materials: information (and people) can be transformed too.

blocks.q: Know how, reputation and work culture are examples of which type of resource?
blocks.explain: Intangible resources include know how, reputation and culture; tangible are physical, human are the people and their skills.

blocks.q: Apple entering the smartphone market with a handheld computer is an example of:
blocks.explain: A radically different approach or new technology that changes how things are done is supply-side disruption (Gans, 2016).

blocks.q: According to Grant (2010), which is NOT one of the four things to think through when putting resources together?
blocks.explain: Grant's four are processes, organisational structure, motivation and alignment.

blocks.q: A resource is valuable and rare but easy for competitors to imitate. According to VIRO, the implication is:
blocks.explain: Y, Y, N on valuable, rare, inimitable gives temporary advantage.

blocks.q: A resource is valuable, rare and inimitable, but the organisation does not exploit it. The implication is:
blocks.explain: Only when the organisation is also organised to exploit the resource do you get sustained advantage.

blocks.q: Key success factors are addressed by asking questions about customers and about competition.
blocks.explain: Grant (2010) suggests asking who customers are and what they want, and who the competition is, the dimensions and the intensity of competition.

chapters.title: Session 7: Financing your business
chapters.summary: Sources of finance, cash flow, financial statements and what investors look for.

blocks.text: One of the main reasons businesses fail is that they run out of cash. Your business model might be sustainable at first through investment of your own money, and over time through retained profits, but it is unlikely you can finance growth and expansion that way indefinitely.

blocks.alt: Chalk sketch of a bar chart with an upward trajectory
blocks.caption: Figure 1 Capturing value in each transaction leads to sustainability

blocks.text: Every business needs to capture some percentage of the value in each transaction. Your key stakeholders (suppliers, customers, distributors, investors, staff) must also see mutual value in the deal.

The key to a sustainable business is **cash flow management**: understanding how and when income and expenditure arise, and forecasting so you can meet financial obligations in the short and long term. By the end of this session you will be able to:

items: recognise alternative sources of finance for a new business and how to choose between them
understand some of the key financial concepts needed when running a business
understand the two most important financial statements you will need to manage your business
recognise ways to improve your cash flow management and sustain your business
understand how investors and lenders evaluate your business when they consider funding it.

blocks.text: This session will not make you a finance expert, but it will help you evaluate the benefits, risks and obligations of each form of finance and have a more informed discussion with a finance professional.
There are three main sources of business funding:

items: **Equity financing** - contributed by the owners at start-up. Equity is never repaid unless the business is closed down and there are enough funds from liquidation. No regular interest is paid, but investors hope for a dividend if the business is profitable.

**Debt financing** - comes from a third party external to the business. The loan must be repaid in full at the end of the loan period, with interest paid on the amount. The lender is first in the queue if the business is made bankrupt. In the UK, interest is currently deducted as an expense from sales revenues before tax is calculated.
**Reinvested profits** - come from the owners, but profits need to materialise as cash to be re-invested or spent supporting the business.

blocks.title: Activity 1 Pros and cons of funding sources
blocks.prompt: Consider what the pros and cons to your business may be of equity financing, debt financing and reinvested profits.
blocks.model: How you finance your business depends on factors such as whether you are prepared to give away ownership, whether you expect high growth, whether your sales pipeline looks healthy, and whether you have rapid sales turnover with customers who pay on time. There may be other reasons specific to your business.
points: Equity means giving away some ownership and control but does not need repaying
Debt must be repaid with interest but you keep ownership
Reinvested profits depend on profits actually materialising as cash
Choice depends on growth expectations, sales pipeline and how quickly customers pay

blocks.text: A growing business needs to make the most of all its resources, including cash. **Cash management** means assessing the flow of cash in your business and thinking about how to improve it. It considers:

items: the agreements and terms you reach with suppliers and distributors, if applicable
the speed at which you collect money in from customers
the speed at which you pay money to suppliers
the amount of cash you want to keep invested in inventory (the stock of goods held for re-sale).

blocks.text: The first steps in external funding decisions are to evaluate your current cash position, as prospective lenders will do the same.

Sales are usually made on account or on credit, so there is a delay between making the sale and receiving cash. Without enough cash flowing round the business to cover that delay, your enterprise will come to a halt.
Establishing where your cash is committed can be complex:

items: goods may have been bought and paid for in cash
employees involved in manufacturing or operations need to be paid
overheads such as rent, energy or computer costs may already have been paid out.

blocks.text: All of these running costs must be funded before cash is actually received from customers.

blocks.title: Solvency and liquidity
blocks.text: A business remains **solvent** when its cash resources can satisfy its longer-term financial obligations as they fall due. This requires **liquid funds**, i.e. cash, or assets that can be readily transformed into cash. **Liquidity** is the ability of an enterprise to pay its short-term obligations. Good management of working capital helps ensure that profits do become cash.

blocks.q: A business can pay its short-term obligations as they fall due. Which term describes this ability?
blocks.explain: Liquidity is the ability of an enterprise to pay its short-term obligations.

pages.title: Working capital and the balance sheet

blocks.text: The day-to-day running costs and operational resources are called **working capital**. A positive figure means current assets (immediate cash and what is owed to the business) exceed current liabilities (what the business owes), which gives suppliers and lenders a sense of security.
Working capital = cash at bank + inventory + cash due from customers (receivables) - cash due to suppliers (payables).
A **balance sheet** summarises the assets and liabilities of a business, and its equity, at a particular moment in time.

items: **Assets** - things a business owns, or money owed to it.
**Liabilities** - financial obligations, or amounts the business owes to somebody else.
**Equity** (sometimes 'net worth') - assets minus liabilities: the value remaining after all obligations are taken into account.

blocks.text: **Depreciation** allocates the cost of an asset over its useful life, so fixed assets such as plant or machinery may appear with declining value in successive years.
The balance sheet indicates financial health: the ability to pay bills when they fall due, cash resources, and how much debt there is in relation to equity.

blocks.alt: Example balance sheet listing current assets, non-current assets, liabilities and stockholders' equity, with totals
blocks.caption: Figure 2 Example of a balance sheet

blocks.q: In the example, total assets are 101,000 and total liabilities 16,000. What is the equity (net worth)?
blocks.explain: Equity = assets minus liabilities = 101,000 - 16,000 = 85,000, matching the stockholders' equity shown.

blocks.text: A **profit and loss account** (p&l), sometimes called an income statement, shows how a business has performed over a period such as a month or a year. It pulls together sales revenues and expenses to show whether a profit or loss was generated, and so whether the business is economically viable.

blocks.alt: Spreadsheet showing an empty example of a profit and loss account with income and expenses in the left column
blocks.caption: Figure 3 Example of a business' profit and loss account

blocks.text: The p&l shows the complete trading picture over time, including sales made before customers have paid. Expenses include *all* costs incurred, even those not yet paid.

items: Sales revenue includes cash sales and sales made on credit terms.
Cost of goods sold includes cash purchases and purchases made on credit terms.

blocks.text: It is a basis for business decisions: owners can see trends in sales, expenses and margins, compare with earlier periods and similar businesses, and budget for the future.

blocks.q: A profit and loss account only includes costs that have already been paid in cash.
blocks.explain: Expenses shown include all costs incurred, including those not yet paid.

blocks.text: A limited company is owned by its shareholders: those who have paid money to acquire a legal and financial interest ('a share'). If you have incorporated (Limited, Ltd or plc) you are protected from taking on the losses of the business, because it is a separate legal entity (see Session 2).

Incorporation protects investors and acts as an incentive to invest: the most a shareholder can lose is their original investment. Shares can be bought and sold without financial impact on the company, other than the legal duty to maintain a register of shareholders.

blocks.title: Reflection: What would you invest in?
blocks.prompt: Take a moment to reflect on what kind of enterprise you might invest in and why. What factors might you take into consideration? What would you expect in return?
blocks.model: You might invest in an enterprise whose founders you trust, where there is clear mutual value, a credible market and evidence of how it makes money. In return you might expect repayments, dividends or growth in the value of your shares, as well as perhaps non-financial returns that match your own values.
points: Consider the people, idea and evidence of demand
Expect a return: repayments, dividends or share value growth
Weigh risk against return
Own values may matter beyond money

blocks.text: Investors seek a return through regular repayments, dividends or an increase in the future value of their shares. They want to understand past performance as an indication of viability. Can you demonstrate your profit margin? It shows how well you control costs, and a higher margin means more resilience to unforeseen events.
Other facts and figures that satisfy investors:

items: your rate of growth compared with your past, competitors and the economy
